    Speaking Part 2

    P2-001

    Advertisements

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe an advertisement that persuaded you to buy a product.

    You should say:

    • What advertisement it was
    • Was it shown on TV, radio or newspaper
    • What was good about that advertisement

    Explain why you think that advertisement made the product seem attractive.

    Answer

    215 words

    The advertisement was for a small folding umbrella, and I saw it on television one evening last autumn. I'd been carrying a rather large umbrella that was useful in the rain and awkward everywhere else, so the product caught my attention straight away.

    The advert followed a woman through an ordinary journey. She put the folded umbrella in a side pocket of her bag, took it out when it started raining and then put it away as she entered a shop. There wasn't much talking. You could see the size of it beside things you recognised, which was more useful to me than simply being told that it was compact.

    What I liked was that it showed the bit after the dramatic moment. The rain had stopped, but she still had an umbrella to carry. That was exactly the small problem I wanted to solve. It also showed how the cover fitted over the wet fabric, so the demonstration seemed quite practical.

    I bought one a few days later, after checking that I could open and close it comfortably. The advertisement made it attractive by putting it into a day I could easily imagine having. I didn't need a more exciting journey; I just wanted less umbrella to carry when the weather was behaving itself.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P2-002

    A Challenging Thing You Did

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a challenging thing you have done.

    You should say:

    • when you did it
    • why you did it
    • how you handled this challenge

    and explain why you thought it was challenging.

    Answer

    228 words

    One challenging thing I did was give a short talk at a local discussion group last spring. The subject was how to decide whether an online explanation was trustworthy. I'd been reading about it and thought I understood it reasonably well, so I volunteered to introduce the discussion.

    Preparing the talk showed me how much I'd been taking for granted. I could follow an argument on the page, but when I tried to explain it aloud, I kept stopping to define another word. My ten-minute talk was becoming an introduction to an introduction.

    I dealt with that by choosing one simple example: two websites giving different explanations of the same everyday problem. I wrote down the questions I would ask about each one, then removed anything that didn't help answer those questions. A friend listened to me practise and pointed out where she'd lost the thread.

    On the day, I still felt nervous, especially when someone asked something I hadn't prepared for. I said I wasn't sure and asked them to explain their concern. That gave us a useful discussion instead of a long, doubtful answer from me.

    The challenge was making my understanding available to other people. I couldn't rely on recognising the ideas myself. By the end, people were discussing the example without needing me to keep explaining it, and that felt like a good result.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P2-004

    A Person You Know

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a child that you know and like a lot.

    You should say:

    • Who the child is
    • How do you know them
    • What do they enjoy doing

    Explain why you like them a lot.

    Answer

    229 words

    I'd like to talk about my neighbour's daughter, Hana. She's eight, and I've known her for about three years because our families sometimes have lunch together. I also see her when she's playing outside near the flats.

    She enjoys drawing and making little buildings out of cardboard. The buildings usually start as houses, but they don't stay that way for long. A bedroom becomes a shop, then the shop needs a station, and by the time she's finished there's an entire town across the floor.

    What I like about her is how seriously she considers other people's suggestions. Once, I asked how the people in her town would get from the station to their houses. She looked at it for a moment, moved two buildings and made a road from a strip of paper. Then she explained that the road had been missing because she hadn't finished yet. I thought that was a very fair answer.

    She's also kind in quite practical ways. If another child wants to join in, she'll find them something to make rather than simply telling them to watch. She can certainly be impatient when a roof keeps falling off, but she usually returns to it.

    I enjoy spending time with her because her ideas keep changing in ways I couldn't have predicted. I never quite know what I'll be asked to help build next.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P2-014

    Animal

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe an interesting animal you have seen.

    You should say:

    • What animal it was
    • When and Where you saw it
    • And explain how you feel about this animal

    and explain why you think this animal is interesting.

    Answer

    232 words

    The animal I'd choose is a heron I saw beside a river last autumn. I was walking through a park early in the morning, and at first I thought it was part of a branch sticking out of the water. It was standing so still that I nearly passed it without noticing.

    Then it turned its head, and the whole shape suddenly made sense. It had long thin legs, grey feathers and a neck folded into a rather neat curve. I stopped some distance away and watched. There were people running along the path behind me, but the bird seemed entirely occupied with one small patch of water.

    After a while, it moved its head forward very quickly and came up with a small fish. The movement was so different from the stillness before it that I almost missed it. A moment later, it was standing quietly again.

    I found it interesting because I'd normally look for movement when trying to spot an animal. This one made me pay attention to something that appeared to be doing nothing. Of course, I couldn't know exactly what it was watching, but the sudden movement suggested that it had been paying close attention.

    I felt lucky to have stopped. The rest of the walk was a little slower, mainly because I kept checking the edges of the river for another shape I might have overlooked.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P2-015

    Art

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Talk about a painting you would like to have in your home.

    You should say:

    • what is it
    • how you know about it
    • how much it would cost you

    and explain why you want to have it in your home.

    Answer

    230 words

    I'd like to have a small watercolour of a harbour that I saw at an exhibition in our community centre a few weeks ago. It was by a local artist, and it showed a row of boats early in the morning, before anyone seemed to have started work.

    Most of the painting was in soft blue and grey, but there was one yellow boat near the front. What caught my attention was its reflection. The boat itself was quite clearly drawn, while the yellow in the water had broken into little uneven shapes. I kept moving closer to look at that, then stepping back to see the whole harbour again.

    The price on the card was a hundred and forty pounds. That would be a considered purchase for me, so I didn't buy it immediately. I'd need to set some money aside, and I'd also want to check that it would fit in the space beside my desk.

    I'd like it there because it gives me a feeling of room to breathe without being completely empty. There are ropes, windows and small marks to notice when you look carefully. From across the room, though, it's simply a quiet morning by the water.

    I think I'd enjoy having those two views available: something calm to see when I look up, and something more detailed to return to when I have time.

    • what you were doing
    • who apologised to you

    Answer

    223 words

    This happened last winter, when a friend called Ben came round to return a book I'd lent him. I was sitting at the kitchen table, putting notes in order for a course, and he placed the book beside them rather carefully.

    Before I opened it, he told me he'd spilt coffee over a few pages. He apologised straight away and said he'd already looked for another copy. I remember noticing that he was holding the book by the clean edge, as though that might make the accident a little smaller.

    I was disappointed because I'd written some notes in the margins, so a new copy wouldn't have replaced everything. We looked through it together, though, and most of the writing was still clear. A few pages had become slightly wavy, but they weren't stuck together.

    I told him I'd keep that copy and that he could buy me a coffee instead. He laughed, then asked whether I was sure. I appreciated that he checked rather than assuming the joke meant I didn't care about the damage.

    What mattered was that he'd told me before I discovered it myself and offered a practical way to put things right. I still have the book, and the marked pages are easy to find. Whenever I reach them, I remember the careful way he set it down.

    Answer

    230 words

    A book I finished recently was Through the Looking-Glass by Lewis Carroll. It follows Alice as she steps through a mirror and enters a world organised partly like a game of chess. She travels across it, meets various characters and eventually becomes a queen, although reaching that position doesn't make everything easier to understand.

    I enjoyed it, especially the way ordinary words can suddenly create an unusual problem. The characters may sound quite certain, but if you follow what they're saying carefully, the meaning sometimes changes underneath the conversation. I found myself slowing down at moments that initially looked very simple.

    My favourite section was Alice's meeting with the White Knight. His inventions and his difficulties with riding are funny, but the scene also feels unusually gentle. He tries to be helpful, and Alice listens to him. I liked that the book gave their farewell time to matter instead of rushing directly to the next strange event.

    I'll probably read it again. The first time, I was often wondering where Alice would go next. On another reading, I'd pay more attention to the sentences and to how a scene changes from something comic into something quiet.

    It's also a book I could return to in small sections. I don't think remembering the events would remove the pleasure, because quite a lot of it comes from how those events are told.

Our instructor was patient, though, and she kept giving me one manageable thing to work on. I didn't have to think about crossing the whole pool immediately.

    The change happened gradually. At first, I was pleased simply to move away from the side. Later, I could swim a short distance without stopping to check where the edge was. I still remember finishing a length and turning round because I wanted to see the distance from the other end.

    Since then, swimming has become something I can choose to do for pleasure. I sometimes go early at the weekend, when the pool is quieter. On holidays, I also feel less excluded when friends suggest going for a swim, although I still stay within what I'm comfortable doing.

    It affected my life in a fairly ordinary but lasting way. A place where I used to feel awkward is now somewhere I enjoy spending an hour. I don't have to invent a reason to remain beside the steps.

    I decided to stay and finish the course before looking again. It was important because I was choosing how to spend the next few years, rather than just comparing two salaries. It makes the path unpleasant, and broken glass can make particular spots unsafe to use. Some of the bins fill up, while other rubbish appears to have been dropped well away from any picnic area. I wouldn't assume it all comes from the same source.

    I think the area could improve if regular collection, suitable bins and local clean-ups worked together. People also need a clear reason to care for the place between organised events. If the response remains occasional, I expect the same patches to fill up again. I'd like to see a future visit where I notice the river first, instead of immediately looking for the next piece of packaging.

    The social part matters too. We usually have a drink afterwards and talk for a few minutes before going home. It gives the weekend a pleasant beginning without taking up the whole day. I tend to leave feeling that I've used my body and given my thoughts a different job for a while.

    It was exciting because the view was familiar in its separate parts and completely unfamiliar as a whole. I also felt nervous at first, though the pilot explained what was happening. When we landed, I was pleased to feel solid ground again. For the rest of the day, I kept looking up at the sky, remembering that we'd been part of someone else's distant view.

    The map showed places that meant something to us: the café where we usually met, a park bench and the station where one of us was nearly always waiting for the other. I drew it by hand and added little notes beside the places. It wasn't accurate enough to help a stranger find their way, but Leah recognised everything immediately.

    I chose it because she already had plenty of things to pack, and a small flat frame wouldn't take much space. More importantly, it gathered memories that would have been difficult to put into an ordinary card. When she opened it, she pointed to the station first and asked whether I'd marked the correct entrance this time.

    Compared with other gifts I've given her, it took more time and less money. I'd bought her books before, which she enjoyed, but this was made specifically for her. I liked that she could explain every odd little mark to someone else, if she wanted to, while keeping some of the stories to herself.

    I liked the scale of the suggestions. A walk to the shops or a regular walk with a friend is something a person can picture doing. The article made me look at my own day and notice where a short walk might fit. I began taking a slightly longer route home from a nearby shop when I had time.

    I think the article could help people's health because it connects a general benefit with actions that can be repeated. Of course, people's abilities and circumstances differ, so the same routine won't suit everyone. For me, its value was making the first step feel manageable. I also found the displays helpful because some of the remains would have meant very little to me without an explanation.     I enjoyed the visit because the place kept changing in my mind as I learnt more. At first, I mainly noticed its size and age. Later, I began to picture it as somewhere people had actually used.     When I was a child, I spent a lot of my free time drawing little comics. I started at about eight, after my older brother showed me a book of short cartoon stories. I liked the idea that a few pictures could tell a story, even when the drawings were very simple.

    For the next five or six years, I filled cheap exercise books with them. Most were about two children who were trying to solve very small problems, like finding a missing shoe. The search could last several pages, although the shoe usually turned out to be somewhere obvious. I drew at the kitchen table, and sometimes my brother would suggest what should happen next. I didn't always accept his suggestions, which was probably part of the attraction.

    I enjoyed deciding what readers would see in each picture. If I drew the missing object in a corner before the characters noticed it, the reader could be ahead of them for a moment. That felt surprisingly powerful when I was small.

    I'm less interested in making comics now, mainly because I spend more time reading and doing other things. I still sketch occasionally, though, and I kept a couple of those old books. The drawings are awkward, but I can remember exactly what I found funny when I made them.

    Language

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Talk about one method of learning a foreign language you have used.

    You should say:

    • What you did
    • How long have you used this method for
    • How it compares to other methods of learning a language

    And say if you will use that same method in the future or not, and why

    Answer

    238 words

    One method I've used is taking a short English conversation and changing the situation behind it. I tried this quite regularly for about four months, usually for fifteen or twenty minutes at a time.

    I'd begin with a few lines that I could understand comfortably. Then I'd make brief notes about what the speakers were doing: asking for an explanation, giving a reason or making a suggestion. After that, I'd change one thing. Perhaps the suggestion would no longer be possible, or the person replying would need more information before agreeing.

    The interesting part was discovering that changing the situation didn't always mean changing many words. Sometimes a small addition made the difference quite clear. On other occasions, I produced a perfectly tidy sentence that answered the wrong question. I'd read it aloud, imagine hearing it as the other person, and realise why it didn't quite fit.

    Compared with learning separate word lists, this gave the words a job to do. Compared with copying a whole dialogue, it made me decide what I actually wanted to communicate. I still needed grammar explanations when I couldn't see how to make a change, so it didn't replace other study completely.

    I intend to keep using it, but with less of the original conversation in front of me. I'd like to start from a situation, say something myself, and then use the reference to see what I could express more clearly.

    I'd choose Lake Biwa, which is in Shiga Prefecture in Japan. It's the country's largest lake, covering roughly six hundred and seventy square kilometres. Those figures are quite hard to picture until you're standing beside it.

It's also a habitat for many kinds of plants and animals. So protecting its water matters to people who may never go there for a walk.

    For visitors, it offers space to be outdoors without every moment needing an activity. I remember sitting near the shore while a family further along tried to take a photograph with everyone looking in the same direction. Behind that small performance, the water went on moving quietly.

    That's the impression I have of it: a beautiful place that people enjoy, and an essential part of ordinary life far beyond the view from the bank.

    It was good news because it gave her an opportunity she wanted and changed something for our family too. We wouldn't need a whole weekend to see each other. We could meet for dinner on a Wednesday, or go for a walk without arranging it weeks ahead. That's the part I'm most looking forward to.

    Two people I think are very good parents are my friends Tom and Aisha. They have a seven-year-old son, and I met them about four years ago when we helped organise a local gardening event. We stayed in touch, and I sometimes spend a weekend afternoon with them.

    What I admire is the attention they give their son without making him the centre of every decision. If he asks a question, they usually stop and answer it, or explain when they'll have time. They also give him small jobs to do. During one visit, he was helping make lunch and became upset because he'd dropped some tomatoes on the floor. Aisha helped him pick them up, then gave him something else to prepare. The accident didn't become the whole afternoon.

    Tom is good at admitting when he's misunderstood something. Once, he apologised after blaming his son for moving a tool that he'd actually put away himself. He said it quite plainly and carried on. I liked that, because the child could see that being the adult didn't mean always being right.

    I think good parenting requires that combination of care, clear expectations and willingness to listen. Children need boundaries, but they also need room to make ordinary mistakes. From what I've seen, Tom and Aisha give their son both, and they seem to enjoy his company as a person.

At first, people stayed with whoever they already knew, but then Priya couldn't find the serving spoons. Several of us started opening the boxes she'd labelled for the kitchen.     Later, her brother put on some music and we played a game where we had to draw things for the others to guess. One drawing was supposed to be a bicycle, but it looked so much like a pair of spectacles that the answer became an argument of its own. By that point, nobody was sitting in their original group.

    I enjoyed it because people gradually became comfortable together, without anyone having to make a big effort to entertain us. Priya seemed pleased to have the flat full of voices after several evenings of unpacking alone. When I helped wash up at the end, we finally found the spoons in a box beside the sink. They'd been within reach all evening.

    • what it is used for

    Answer

    236 words

    I'd talk about washi, which is traditional Japanese paper. There are different kinds, including paper made by machine, but the handmade version is the one I find most interesting. It's used for things such as artwork, lanterns and the paper panels in traditional sliding doors.

    In broad terms, making it starts with plant fibres, often from the bark of a shrub called kozo. The material is cleaned, cooked and beaten so that the fibres separate. These are mixed with water and a plant-based liquid that helps them remain suspended. The maker lifts the mixture with a screen held in a frame and moves it carefully to spread the fibres into a sheet. The sheets are then pressed and dried.

    What interests me is how much depends on controlled movement. A sheet can look very simple once it's finished, but getting the fibres evenly spread takes skill. I once watched a demonstration and found myself following the movement of the frame rather than looking at the finished paper on the table.

    Japan produces it partly because the materials and water resources supported papermaking, and because the skills have been passed on through generations. There are also continuing uses for it in art and buildings. I like that connection between a traditional process and something people can still put to practical use. It's a craft you can understand a little better by looking closely at one ordinary sheet.

    My favourite book is Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll. I first read it as an adult about two years ago, although I already knew some of the characters from pictures and adaptations. I wanted to find out what the original story was actually like.

    It's about Alice following a rabbit and entering a strange world where her size changes and ordinary conversations become unexpectedly difficult. She's often trying to do something quite reasonable, such as reach a garden or understand an explanation, while the people she meets make the situation more complicated.

    What I enjoy most is how the writing keeps those small practical concerns visible. At the tea party, for instance, there are peculiar arguments, but there are also cups, seats and the difficulty of getting a straightforward answer. I can follow the scene even when the rules are odd. The humour often grows out of the characters taking something too literally or refusing to notice what another person means.

    I also like the quieter ending, when Alice is back beside her sister and the world around them feels ordinary again. The book leaves me with more than the amusing conversations. I remember movements, sounds and small changes in what Alice notices. It's my favourite because I can enjoy it as a story and then return to a familiar passage just to see how the sentences work.

    A traffic rule I know is the requirement to stop at a red traffic light. I'm thinking of the ordinary traffic signals described in Britain's Highway Code: drivers wait behind the stop line, and a green light allows them to move only if the way is clear.

    I learnt the basic meaning of the colours as a child, but I paid much more attention to the details when I took driving lessons. My instructor made me look beyond the light itself. It wasn't enough to notice that a signal had changed; I also needed to see what was happening at the junction.

    I follow the rule when I drive. I remember waiting once at a quiet junction in the evening, with no car immediately in front of me. A cyclist then came across from the side road. It made the arrangement quite easy to understand: while I was waiting, someone else could use the same space.

    The rule is important because people need a shared basis for anticipating one another's movements. If each driver decided independently when a red light could be ignored, the cyclist or pedestrian would have far less certainty. The signals don't remove the need to pay attention, but they organise a complicated meeting of routes. I find it easier to be patient when I think about that whole junction, rather than only the stretch of road ahead of my car.

    A subject I'd like to study is cognitive science, particularly how people form concepts and use them to understand unfamiliar situations. What attracts me is the gap between recognising an answer and being able to explain how you reached it.

When my friend suggested a different grouping, I had to work out what my own rule actually was. The discussion became more interesting than the game.

    I'd like to learn how researchers investigate things such as memory, attention and language, and how they distinguish a plausible explanation from one supported by an experiment. I'm also interested in what computer models can contribute without assuming that a machine and a person must solve a problem in the same way.

    It's possible to study the subject at universities, either through cognitive science programmes or through related areas such as psychology, linguistics and computing. I'd want a course that gave me a solid introduction to research methods as well as the larger questions.

    I think I'll begin studying it informally quite soon, with an introductory course and some reading. A full degree would take more preparation and a clearer decision about where to study.     Describe a problem in your city.

    • what it is
    • how serious it is
    • what causes this problem

    and say what can be done to solve or reduce the effects of this problem.

    Answer

    242 words

    One problem in my city is that pavements around the main station are often partly blocked. There are bicycles left against railings, advertising boards outside shops and sometimes stacks of delivery boxes. Individually, each object takes up a fairly small space. Together, they can leave very little room to walk.

    I think it's quite serious in the busiest streets. Most people can squeeze past, but that isn't an adequate arrangement for everyone. I once saw someone pushing a pushchair reach a narrow gap, stop and turn back to find another route. Someone using a wheelchair could face the same difficulty. At busy times, people also step towards the road to pass one another.

    Several things seem to contribute. Some pavements are narrow to begin with, and there aren't enough convenient places to leave bicycles near the station. Shops need deliveries, but there isn't a clear shared arrangement for where boxes can wait. I wouldn't put the entire problem down to people being inconsiderate; the space gives them few easy options.

    The city could provide better bicycle parking and agree clear delivery arrangements with businesses. It should also keep a continuous walking route free of obstacles, with regular checks rather than one occasional clear-out. Residents and shopkeepers need to know which areas must remain open. I would judge improvement by whether someone can complete the whole route comfortably, including at its narrowest point, rather than by how tidy one newly cleared corner looks.

What made it difficult was coordinating several unfamiliar actions that an experienced person seemed to do as one. The machine itself hadn't become simpler; I'd begun to recognise what needed my attention.

    Answer

    234 words

    I'd choose sushi, a traditional Japanese food that's still very popular in Japan. There are several forms, but the familiar ones use rice seasoned with vinegar, combined with ingredients such as fish, egg or vegetables. It isn't simply another name for raw fish.

    For a basic roll, the rice is cooked and mixed with a vinegar seasoning. It is spread over a sheet of seaweed, fillings are placed along it, and the whole thing is rolled and cut into pieces. Another common form has a topping laid over a small shaped portion of rice. The idea is easy to describe, although making everything the right size and texture takes practice.

    I think part of its popularity is the variety. People can choose different ingredients and amounts, and it can suit an ordinary meal as well as a special occasion. In my family, we sometimes buy a mixed selection to share. Someone always changes their mind about which piece they want once the box is open, so choosing can take nearly as long as eating.

    It's popular in other countries too, and sushi has spread well beyond Japan. That doesn't mean every version is the same or that everyone likes the same ingredients. For me, the attraction is that a recognisable basic form leaves plenty of room for different choices. A shared plate can be familiar while still giving each person something they particularly enjoy.

It felt like an ordinary morning journey that happened to be taking place on water.

    Once we were moving, I went outside. The buildings behind us seemed to gather into a single shape, while the town ahead slowly separated into roofs, windows and individual streets. I took a few photographs, then put my phone away because I kept missing things while looking at the pictures I'd just taken. For most of the journey, I simply watched.

    I felt unusually calm when we arrived. I hadn't been doing anything especially restful; there had been engine noise, wind and people moving about. But the gradual change of view had held my attention. My friend was waiting near the landing, and I remember wanting to tell her about the crossing before we'd even started talking about our plans for the day.

    Travel

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a holiday that you recently went on that you enjoyed.

    You should say:

    • Where you went
    • Who you went with
    • What you did

    Explain why this holiday was enjoyable.

    Answer

    229 words

    A holiday I really enjoyed was a three-night stay in a small seaside town on the south coast of England last spring. I went with my friend Maya. We rented two rooms above a cafe, close enough to the beach that we could hear the wind against the windows at night.

    We hadn't made a detailed plan. On the first morning, we walked along the shore, collected a few smooth stones to look at and put them back before returning for lunch. Later, we visited a small local museum and spent longer than expected looking at old photographs of the town. Maya kept finding buildings we'd already passed, so the walk back became a kind of search. One doorway was still there, almost hidden by a bright new shopfront. The next day we took a bus to a nearby village, had tea and walked back along a footpath before the light began to fade.

    What made it enjoyable was how easily we agreed about the pace. If one of us wanted to stop, there was usually something for the other to notice too. We had proper conversations, but we were also comfortable walking without talking. On the last morning, we sat outside the cafe with our bags beside us and watched the same street wake up. I was sorry to leave, mainly because it had started to feel familiar.

    Traditional Product

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a traditional product in your country.

    You should say:

    • what the product is
    • when you tried this product for the first time
    • what it is made of

    and explain how you feel about it.

    Answer

    225 words

    A traditional Japanese product I'd choose is a furoshiki, which is a square cloth used for wrapping and carrying things. The one I use is made of cotton, although they can be made from other materials, including silk. Mine is dark blue with a small white pattern, so it looks quite plain until you unfold it.

    I first tried using one about five years ago at a craft workshop in a community centre. We were given a cloth and an empty lunch box, and the instructor showed us how to wrap it. My first attempt left one corner sticking out and the knot sitting at a rather doubtful angle. She asked me to turn the box slightly and try again. With almost the same movements, the whole thing suddenly looked tidy.

    Since then, I've used that cloth to carry lunch and occasionally to wrap a small present. I like the fact that its shape isn't fixed around one particular object. When I've finished using it, it becomes a flat square again and takes up very little room. I also enjoy seeing different parts of the pattern appear as it's folded.

    I feel quite attached to it now. It reminds me of the patient instructor, but it isn't something I have to keep untouched. Every time I fold it away, it's ready for another ordinary job.

    TV

    Describe a TV programme that you often watch.

    • What kind of programme it is
    • Why you watch it
    • When and why you first started watching it

    And say if you think that programme is better than other TV programmes that are on at the same time or not, and why

    Answer

    228 words

    A programme I often watch is The Repair Shop. It's a factual television programme in which skilled craftspeople restore damaged objects that have a personal meaning for their owners. I usually watch a recorded episode at the weekend, when I have time to follow the work without doing something else at the same time.

    I first started watching about two years ago, after a friend recommended it. She knew I enjoyed seeing how ordinary things were made, and thought the careful repair work would interest me. She was right. I like following the process from the first examination to the moment when the owner sees the object again.

    The technical work and the personal story give each other a purpose. A worn surface may be something to repair, but it can also be part of what makes an object familiar. I find those decisions interesting: what should be replaced, what can be saved, and what ought to remain visible? The programme makes me pay attention to details I would probably have walked past in a shop.

    If it's on at the same time as a quiz or a panel show, I'd usually choose it. That's a personal preference, rather than a claim that the other programmes are worse. I enjoy the slower pace and the sense that a small, careful action is gradually changing something we can see.

    Vegetables

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a plant, vegetable or crop that you are familiar with.

    You should say:

    • Where it grows
    • Why is it important
    • What you like or dislike about it

    And explain why it is important for your country.

    Answer

    231 words

    The crop I'm most familiar with is rice. It's grown in many parts of Japan, and I know it particularly from the paddy fields near my grandparents' village. When I visited as a child, those fields were part of almost every walk we took.

    I remember how different they looked through the growing season. At one point, the water reflected the sky between the young plants. Later, the green seemed to fill the whole field, and you noticed the wind moving across it. At home, rice usually arrived in a bowl without any of that landscape around it, so visiting the village helped me connect the food with the place it came from.

    Rice is important in Japan because it's a staple food and a crop on which farming communities depend. It also belongs to familiar meals and occasions. A simple rice ball can be something you take on a journey, while a bowl of rice can sit beside several quite different dishes at dinner.

    What I like is its quiet place in a meal. It goes with many things without having to be the strongest flavour. I don't enjoy it much when it has become dry, but freshly cooked rice is something I rarely get tired of. For me, its importance is both practical and personal: it feeds people, and it connects an ordinary dinner with a landscape I remember.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P2-130

    Weather

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe a time when the weather prevented you from doing something.

    You should say:

    • what your plan was
    • what weather you were hoping for
    • what happened

    and explain how you felt when you had to change your plans.

    Answer

    230 words

    Last summer, I planned to take a picnic to a park with two friends. We'd chosen a spot beside a small lake and agreed that each of us would bring part of the lunch. I was hoping for a dry, fairly warm afternoon, with enough breeze to make sitting outside comfortable.

    The morning started brightly, but by the time I was packing the food, the sky had become much darker. Then the rain arrived all at once. I stood at the window for a few minutes, hoping it was only a short shower, while the water began running along the edge of the road. One friend sent a photograph of her dripping balcony. After that, none of us tried very hard to defend the picnic plan.

    We met at my flat instead. I was disappointed at first because I'd been looking forward to an afternoon away from familiar rooms. But we moved the small table near the window, spread out the food and made tea. The lunch was probably easier to manage there; nobody had to stop a paper plate from escaping. We talked for a long time, with the rain making a fairly steady sound behind us.

    I still wished we'd been able to go to the lake, but I enjoyed the afternoon. When the rain finally stopped, we opened the window and left the park for another day.

    Work

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe your dream job.

    You should say:

    • What kind of things you would do in that job
    • What the working conditions would be like
    • What kind of workplace you would work in

    And say if you think you will be able to get a job like that or not, and why.

    Answer

    234 words

    My dream job would be designing small exhibitions for a museum, especially exhibitions that help people understand an ordinary object in a new way. I'd work with researchers, choose examples, write clear labels and think about how visitors would move through the space.

    I'd enjoy the mixture of careful reading and practical making. A drawer full of everyday tools might look unremarkable at first, but arranged with the right information, it could show how a job or a household had changed. I'd want to try out the displays with visitors and notice where they stopped, what they asked and which explanation wasn't doing its job.

    The ideal workplace would have a small, cooperative team and somewhere to build rough versions before committing to a finished design. I'd prefer fairly regular hours, with enough flexibility for the busy period before an opening. I wouldn't expect every day to be quietly creative; there would be budgets, deadlines and plenty of adjustments.

    I think I could work towards a role like that, although I'd need relevant training and a stronger collection of practical projects. Volunteering on a small local exhibition would be a realistic first step. What attracts me most is the moment when an arrangement of objects helps someone see a connection for themselves. I wouldn't need every visitor to notice the same thing, but I'd want the display to give them something worth looking at.

    How do (young people) handle difficult or challenging tasks?

    Quite often, they make a difficult task smaller. A student facing a long project might start by finding one useful source, then work out what to do next. Asking a friend or teacher can help too, particularly if they can explain the obstacle clearly. Of course, some people put the whole thing off because they can't see where to begin. I think a useful kind of support is to help them find that first step, then let them take it themselves. Otherwise, the task gets completed, but the person hasn't learnt how to approach the next one.

    P3-006

    A Member of A Team

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Do you think it’s important for children to join teams to learn to cooperate with others?

    Answer

    95 words

    Yes, provided the team gives every child something real to do. In a school play, for example, someone has to listen for a cue, someone has to move a chair, and neither job works very well if everyone acts independently. That makes cooperation visible. But putting children in a group doesn't automatically teach it; one confident child may do all the talking while the others wait. An adult can help by sharing responsibility and making room for quieter contributions. Sports are useful, but a play or a small building project can teach the same lesson.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-012

    Advertisements

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What factors should be taken into account when making advertisements?

    Answer

    93 words

    I'd begin with the audience and the actual purpose of the advert. A message about a local repair service needs different information from one introducing a new game. Then there's accuracy: people should be able to understand what they're being offered, including any important conditions. The setting matters as well. Tiny writing may be readable on a poster you're standing beside and useless on a screen you pass in a second. A clever idea helps people notice an advert, but it also needs to leave them with the right idea about the product.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-017

    Animals

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What should we do to protect endangered animals ?

    Answer

    100 words

    We need to protect the places where animals live, as well as the animals themselves. Saving a few individuals achieves little if they have nowhere suitable to feed or breed. That can mean protecting a forest, reducing pollution in a river, or making it harder to sell threatened wildlife. Local people also need a workable part in the plan. If protecting an area removes their income without offering another option, support may disappear. I'd want clear evidence about the particular species, then measures that can be maintained for years. A brief burst of concern is much easier than steady protection.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-029

    Art

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How has art changed in the past few decades in your country?

    Answer

    102 words

    A change that stands out to me in Japan is how often an artwork first reaches people through a screen. I may see a short video of an installation before I visit the room where it stands. That changes the introduction: the first encounter can be a moving image, a close-up or someone else's response. Older forms, such as painting and pottery, are still part of the picture, so I wouldn't describe it as a simple replacement. My impression is that the routes between artists and audiences have widened, and that can change what people expect to see when they finally arrive.

    Books

    問題へ戻る ↗

    In your opinion, how will e-books affect paper books?

    Answer

    104 words

    I think e-books will take over in some situations rather than make paper books disappear. If you're travelling, carrying several books on one device is convenient, and searching a long text can be useful. With a printed book, though, I like being able to leave a page open and see where a note belongs without moving between screens. Different readers will value those things differently. I can imagine someone reading a novel electronically and later buying a paper copy because they want to keep it. So the two formats may compete, but they can also serve different purposes within the same person's reading life.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-041

    Books

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What’s the difference between films and books?

    Answer

    97 words

    A film usually gives you a shared pace: the scene continues whether you have noticed every detail or not. With a book, you can stop over a sentence, go back, or imagine a room in your own way. Films have other strengths, though. An actor's pause or a sound from outside the frame can suggest something without explaining it. So I wouldn't say books always go deeper and films merely show things. They offer different ways into a story, and an adaptation becomes interesting when it finds a way to create a similar effect through different means.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー

    Business

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do business people relax?

    Answer

    98 words

    I imagine many choose something that breaks the pattern of their working day. Someone who spends hours making decisions might enjoy cooking from a familiar recipe or going for a walk. Others relax by seeing friends, playing sport or simply being somewhere their phone isn't constantly asking for attention. It will depend on the person and on how much free time they have. I wouldn't assume an expensive holiday is the answer. A quiet hour can be quite valuable if it's genuinely their own, especially when the rest of the day has been organised around other people's needs.

    Which do you think is better, to start your own business or to work for someone else?

    Answer

    101 words

    I'd usually prefer to work for someone else first, especially in a field I was still learning about. You can see how decisions, customers and everyday problems fit together before taking responsibility for the whole business. Starting your own offers more control, but that control comes with work you may not particularly enjoy, from chasing payments to arranging cover when someone is ill. It could still be the better choice for a person with a clear idea, useful experience and room to manage uncertainty. For me, the attractive part would be building something worthwhile, rather than simply avoiding having a manager.

    What are some of the major changes that occur to people throughout their lives?

    Answer

    99 words

    Leaving school, starting work, moving home and taking on responsibility for someone else can all change daily life quite sharply. What interests me is that the visible change and the personal adjustment don't always happen together. You can move into a new flat in a day and take months to feel at home there. Some changes are chosen, while others arrive through illness or loss, and the amount of support available makes a difference. So there are familiar stages, but I wouldn't expect everyone to pass through them in the same order or attach the same meaning to them.

There can also be a community you would struggle to find in a smaller place. People may accept a cramped flat or a long journey because those advantages matter more at that stage of their lives. Of course, the balance can change. Once someone has secure work or different family needs, the very noise that made the city feel lively may start to feel exhausting.

People also seem more willing to combine different styles, perhaps a fairly smart jacket with trainers. Online pictures give them plenty of ideas to borrow. I'd be careful about calling every change new, though. A shape that looks fresh to one generation can be something their parents remember wearing, and that makes fashion a rather interesting conversation across time.

I think the strongest reason would be the actual job: who you'd work with, what you'd learn and how much responsibility you'd have. Others have simply become absorbed in a game or a conversation and lose track of time. Those are rather different reasons: one person has chosen the hour, while another only notices it when they look at the clock. I can understand both, although a pleasant evening may be less pleasant in retrospect if it leaves very little time to sleep before the next day's responsibilities.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What are some of the most important decisions young people have to make?

    Answer

    95 words

    Choosing what to study and what kind of work to try are obvious ones, because they affect both time and money. But there are quieter decisions too, such as whom to trust and whether to stay somewhere familiar or move away. I think young people need enough information to make a reasonable choice without feeling they must settle their entire future at once. A short course or some work experience can make an imagined career more real. Discovering that a job doesn't suit you can be useful, especially before you've spent years preparing for it.

    P3-120

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do old people not like changes?

    Answer

    98 words

    Some older people may resist a change because it makes something familiar unnecessarily difficult. If a service moves online, for instance, a person who managed perfectly well yesterday can suddenly need help today. That can feel like losing independence. Past experience may also make people doubtful about another promise that everything will improve. But I wouldn't make this a rule about age; some older people enjoy new methods, and young people can be very attached to their routines. The useful question is what the change asks someone to give up, and whether its benefits are clear to them.

    How are the eating habits now in your country different from eating habits in the past?

    Answer

    100 words

Buying a prepared meal or food that needs very little cooking can fit a busy evening more easily than making everything from scratch. Older accounts of family meals often put more emphasis on preparation at home, though of course that wasn't everybody's life. I wouldn't say familiar food has simply disappeared: a ready-made meal can still contain rice, fish and vegetables. Part of the change concerns who prepares the food and how much time it takes, as well as what finally appears on the plate.

A short activity on a device could show that half the class has made the same mistake, so the teacher can explain that point again before moving on. That seems more useful than simply putting the textbook on a screen. There may also be more individual practice, with different pupils working on different difficulties. But someone still needs to decide what the answers reveal. A pupil can choose the correct option for the wrong reason, and a conversation may be needed to find that out.

    What devices do you think will be popular in the future?

For example, a simple home control that works reliably for people with different needs may be more useful than something with dozens of features nobody can find. Translation devices could also become more attractive if they handle ordinary conversation naturally. But popularity will depend on price, trust and ease of use, not just technical ability. A device that listens all the time may be convenient and still make people uneasy. I suspect the successful ones will fit into daily life without continually asking us to organise life around them.

Concern alone isn't enough, though. People need practical choices, such as usable public transport, so that acting on that concern doesn't depend entirely on having spare time or money.

A participant may enjoy developing skill while trying to keep the risk within limits, whereas someone else may be chasing the thrill. Those motives can overlap, but they're different. So I'd describe the clear change as fewer people under one roof, rather than assume the whole circle of relatives has shrunk by the same amount. Some things remain very local, such as the people preparing food or bringing out equipment together. I'd avoid saying festivals were all more authentic in the past. It can also be convenient for meeting a friend to discuss work. Of course, a crowded table and loud music would have the opposite effect. I think the attraction is a change of setting with just enough company, although it won't suit everyone or every kind of task.

    Why is it that different people want to see different magazines?

So the subject matters, but the purpose and style matter too. A good match gives the reader the kind of attention or escape they're looking for at that moment.

    Answer

    93 words

    They can explain a difficult point, share notes after an absence or help someone find a place in a group. With schoolwork, I think the most useful help leaves the other student able to do something independently. Showing how you approached a maths problem can be better than handing over the answer. There are limits, of course: a friend shouldn't have to become a private teacher every evening. But small, regular acts matter, particularly for a new student who may need someone to explain the ordinary routines that everybody else has stopped noticing.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-261

    History

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What is the effect of technology on how people learn about history?

    Answer

    101 words

    Technology can bring people much closer to historical material. You might read a scanned letter, compare old maps or hear a recorded account without travelling to an archive. That makes it easier to ask your own questions instead of relying entirely on a textbook's selection. But the screen can also make very different sources look equally convincing. An attractive reconstruction is still someone's interpretation, and a short clip may leave out the context that explains it. I think the best use combines access with questions about who made the material, when they made it and what it can actually tell us.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-263

    Holiday

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How important is it for families to go on holiday together?

    Answer

    98 words

    It can be very valuable because family members get time together outside their usual roles. At home, one person may be rushing to work while another is thinking about school; on holiday, they might finally spend a morning doing the same thing. Shared memories can grow from very small moments. Still, I wouldn't make an expensive trip a test of a good family. A day out can provide some of the same space, and a holiday packed with arguments or obligations may provide very little. What matters to me is having time together that people can actually enjoy.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-274

    Home

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How easy is it to find a place to live in your country?

    Answer

    105 words

    It can be difficult if someone needs an affordable place in a particular part of a large Japanese city. The search becomes narrower when you add a short journey to work, enough space and a suitable moving date. In a less crowded area, there may be more room to choose, although that doesn't automatically mean the location will suit the person's life. I'd separate finding an available property from finding a workable home. A place can be empty and still be too far from a job or the people someone relies on. So my answer would depend quite a lot on where and for whom.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-280

    Influence

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why is it important for young people to have role models?

    Answer

    90 words

    A role model can make a possible future easier to imagine. Seeing someone practise, make mistakes and improve gives a young person a more useful picture than simply hearing that success takes effort. It may also show them a route they hadn't considered. I'd hope they could admire particular qualities without feeling they must copy a whole life. The person who inspires their work may have habits or opinions they don't share, and that's perfectly reasonable. Having several examples can leave more room to build a life that suits them.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-286

    Internet

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do you think the Internet will change people’s buying habits in the future?

    Answer

    93 words

    I think more buying may become part of another activity. Someone watching a cooking video could order an ingredient immediately, without making a separate trip to a shop. Regular purchases may also become easier to repeat automatically. That would save effort, but it could make spending less noticeable: the thing arrives before you've properly considered whether you still need it. At the same time, people may become more deliberate about checking reviews and comparing alternatives. I can imagine both habits growing together, with routine purchases happening quickly and important ones receiving more research.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-299

    Job

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do you think AI (artificial intelligence) will affect people’s work?

    Answer

    98 words

    I think AI will change the mix of tasks within many jobs. A person might spend less time preparing a first draft and more time deciding whether it is accurate, relevant and appropriate to use. That could be helpful, but only if there is time and expertise for the checking. Some roles may shrink, while others may gain new responsibilities; I wouldn't expect the change to be even. Employers will also have choices about training and how work is organised. The effect on a worker depends partly on those decisions, not just on what a tool can produce.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-300

    Job

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What would you say are the important factors to consider when choosing a career?

    Answer

    95 words

    I'd look at the daily work before the job title. Would I enjoy the kinds of problems I'd be solving, and could I become reasonably good at them? Pay, security, working hours and location matter too, because a career has to fit into the rest of a life. Then I'd consider opportunities to learn and change direction. A role that looks impressive from a distance may involve a routine you dislike, while an unfamiliar job may suit you very well. Talking to people who actually do the work can bring that distance down quite quickly.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-306

    Late

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What is an example of a time when it is very important for people to arrive on time in your country?

    Answer

    89 words

    An entrance exam is a clear example in Japan. If you arrive late, you may miss instructions, lose working time and begin in a hurry while everyone else has settled down. Even without assuming a particular rule about late entry, that's a serious disadvantage. I'd plan to arrive with enough time to find the room and deal with a small delay on the journey. The useful goal is to be ready when the exam begins, which involves a little more than reaching the building at the last possible moment.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-312

    Leisure activities

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why is it important for people to have time for leisure activities?

    Answer

    101 words

    Because people need room for interests that aren't completely defined by work or obligation. A person might play music, grow something or spend an afternoon with friends simply because they enjoy it. Leisure can also give the day a different pace: attention that has been fixed on a difficult problem can move to something else for a while. I think that change can be refreshing, but I wouldn't justify every hobby by saying it will make someone a better worker afterwards. Enjoyment, curiosity and companionship already have value. People should have some time in which the next task isn't deciding everything.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-325

    Machine

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How have these machines benefited people? Are there any negative effects of using them?

    Answer

    100 words

    Household machines, especially washing machines, take over work that would otherwise demand quite a lot of time and effort. You can put a wash on and get on with something else; you don't have to stand there doing every movement yourself. That can be particularly useful when someone has limited strength or a busy household. The disadvantages are the cost, the energy they use and the trouble of getting them repaired. A home can become organised around a machine so completely that one breakdown rearranges everybody's day. So the benefit depends partly on whether the machine stays affordable and repairable.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-327

    Machine

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Let’s move on to technology. Do you think people rely too much on technology?

    Answer

    93 words

    Sometimes, but I wouldn't judge it simply by how often a person uses a device. Technology can make an activity possible for someone, so relying on it isn't automatically a weakness. I'd worry more when people stop noticing what it is doing for them. If a navigation app fails, for example, do I still know roughly where I am, or how to ask for directions? A backup matters more in some situations than others. For me, sensible use means understanding the help you're getting and knowing what to do when it isn't available.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-333

    Memory

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Which do you think is more important to remember, a business meeting or a meeting with a friend?

    Answer

    100 words

    I'd look at who's relying on me, rather than rank the meetings just by their names. Forgetting a business meeting could hold up several people's work, so there may be quite a serious cost. But a friend who's asked to meet because they're having a difficult time may need me just as much. I wouldn't regard that promise as less important because nobody is paying me to keep it. In practice, I'd put both in my diary. If I had to change one, I'd consider the consequences and contact the person early, so they had time to make other arrangements.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-339

    Mobile phones

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What (minimum) age do you think is appropriate for owning a cell phone?

    Answer

    101 words

    For a personal mobile with internet access, I'd suggest around twelve or thirteen as a starting point, with an adult helping to set it up. That's a judgement about responsibility, though, not a birthday at which everyone suddenly becomes ready. A younger child travelling alone might need a basic phone to call home. Before giving wider access, I'd want them to know what to do if a stranger contacts them, how to put the phone away and when to ask for help. I'd introduce those freedoms gradually. Owning the device and being left to manage everything on it are different decisions.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-341

    Money

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What is the relationship between money and power?

    Answer

    96 words

    Money can give people more room to act. They can pay for advice, support an organisation or spend time on a problem without worrying immediately about earning a living. Those choices can become influence over other people. But money and authority aren't quite the same thing. A wealthy person may fund a project and still need others to trust them or agree to take part. People with very little money can also gain influence by organising together. I'd say money often makes power easier to acquire, while rules and relationships affect how far that power reaches.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-351

    Music

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What are some possible advantages and disadvantages of being stricter about the illegal downloading of music?

    Answer

    102 words

    Being stricter could encourage more people to pay for music, which may help the people who create it keep working. The gain would depend on how that money is shared, of course. There are costs as well: checking downloads takes resources, and a mistaken accusation can be difficult for an ordinary listener to challenge. I'd want enforcement to focus on serious unauthorised distribution, with clear information and a fair way to correct errors. Affordable legal access matters too. Protecting the work is more likely to succeed when listening legally is a straightforward choice, rather than a puzzle about what each service allows.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-361

    News

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do you think people will get their news in the future?

    Answer

    102 words

    I expect people will have more choice about how a news report reaches them: a short audio update while they're travelling, a summary on a phone, then a longer account if the subject interests them. Some services may put together a different selection for each reader. That could be convenient, although it might also make it easier to miss an important story outside your usual interests. I hope the original reporting stays easy to find. If a short summary raises a question, you should be able to follow it back to the source, rather than meet another summary of the same summary.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-372

    Parenting

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Do you think mothers and fathers have different roles to play in bringing up a child?

    Answer

    96 words

    They may take on different roles, but I don't think the division has to follow gender. One parent might be good at explaining homework, while the other is better at helping a worried child talk things through. Working hours and experience matter too. What I'd avoid is an arrangement where one parent only gives instructions and the other does all the everyday care. Both need chances to know the child beyond those fixed roles. Different personalities can be valuable, as long as the parents discuss important decisions and the child can turn to either of them.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-381

    Party

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do some people think that national celebrations are a waste of government money? Do you agree or disagree with this view? Why?

    Answer

    98 words

    Some people look at a large celebration and see money that could have paid for something people need every day. If a town is struggling to maintain basic services, an expensive display may seem hard to justify. I understand that objection, but I wouldn't dismiss all national celebrations. A modest public event can give people a shared occasion without requiring them to buy a ticket or organise it themselves. I'd judge the cost against that purpose. Spending more on a grander display doesn't necessarily make the occasion more meaningful, and the budget should be open to public scrutiny.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-384

    Personal

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why are many young people unwilling to listen to their parent’s advice?

    Answer

    95 words

    Sometimes the advice arrives before the young person feels their problem has been understood. They may hear 'You should do this' as another decision being made for them, even if the parent means to help. They may also think the advice comes from circumstances that no longer match their own. That doesn't make the advice wrong, but it helps explain the resistance. I think a question such as 'What have you tried?' can open a better conversation. Parents can offer experience while leaving room for the young person to explain what is different this time.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-420

    Plans

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do most people plan their futures in their education and careers?

    Answer

    101 words

    Often they start with a direction, then work backwards to find the next step. Someone interested in engineering might compare courses, check entry requirements and think about how to pay for the study. Talking to people doing the job can make the plan more realistic. Some people have a detailed route in mind, while others try a course or a first job and adjust as they learn more. I think that second stage matters: a plan made from a prospectus can look different after an ordinary working day. People need room to revise the route without treating every change as failure.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-426

    Products

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What are the disadvantages of a country producing everything it needs?

    Answer

    99 words

    It could make ordinary goods much more expensive. A country would have to put money and skilled workers into activities that other places can carry out more easily. Growing certain fruit in a cold climate, for instance, might need costly protected conditions. Producing everything could also leave less room to specialise and learn from outside suppliers. There would be fewer opportunities to exchange what one place does well for what another does well. Keeping some essential production at home can be sensible, but trying to make every item locally would stretch resources across a very wide range of tasks.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-434

    Restaurants

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What’s the difference between restaurant food and home-cooked food?

    Answer

    99 words

    Restaurant food is usually planned for a range of customers, so consistency, presentation and a clear menu matter. A chef may also have equipment or ingredients that would be impractical in a small home kitchen. At home, you've got more freedom to change the portion, leave something out or use what needs eating. The result may be less polished but exactly what you wanted that evening. I wouldn't divide the two into good and bad food. A restaurant can introduce you to an unfamiliar dish, while an ordinary meal at home can carry years of familiar tastes and habits.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-435

    Rules

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do we have rules in society?

    Answer

    91 words

    Rules help people know what to expect from one another. A queue, for instance, gives strangers a way to take turns without negotiating the whole arrangement every time someone arrives. Rules can also protect people who would otherwise have little power to object. But they need to be understandable and open to challenge. If a rule keeps causing an unfair result, saying 'That's the rule' doesn't explain why we should keep it. I think a society needs both shared expectations and a way to improve them when experience shows a problem.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-443

    School

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What changes do you think will happen in the classrooms of the near future?

    Answer

    95 words

    I think more classrooms will be arranged so that pupils can move between different kinds of work. There might be tables that are easy to move, space for a small group to build something and a quieter corner for reading. A lesson could begin with everyone listening, then spread into several activities before the class comes together again. That would give the room a different rhythm. It would still need clear routines, especially when people are moving about. In the near future, small changes to furniture and storage seem more likely than rebuilding every school.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-445

    School

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Which is more important, research or teaching?

    Answer

    101 words

    It depends on the purpose of the institution and the role we're discussing. For a student trying to understand a first-year course, good teaching is the immediate need. A research result doesn't explain itself to that student. Research matters because it develops and tests the knowledge that future teaching may draw on, but being good at one activity doesn't guarantee being good at the other. I'd want a university to support both and recognise their different demands. When appointing someone mainly to teach, the ability to help students learn should carry real weight, rather than being assumed from a publication list.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-454

    Science

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Which area of science has been the most important in the last one hundred years?

    Answer

    94 words

    I'd choose medical science, especially research into infections. Penicillin was discovered in 1928, and the work that later made it a usable medicine changed treatment for many bacterial infections. That seems a strong example of science making a practical difference to ordinary lives. I'm judging importance by the chance it gives people to recover and carry on living, rather than by how impressive a discovery looks. Of course, medicine relies on chemistry, engineering and other fields, so the boundary isn't neat. Still, if I had to name one area, that's the one I'd choose.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-462

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do some people prefer to purchase brand name products produced abroad?

    Answer

    94 words

    They may associate a foreign brand with a particular design or a reputation for quality. A product that's less common at home can also feel distinctive, and owning it may say something about the image a person wants to present. Advertising can strengthen those associations. Someone buying a bag, for example, might be choosing its shape, the name on it or a little of both. I'd be careful about assuming that an imported label proves better quality. The attraction can be real even when the buyer hasn't compared how well the products are made.

    P3-466

    Social Problems

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What about poverty? What can be done to alleviate poverty?

    Answer

    97 words

    I think support has to work on two timescales. A household that can't cover rent or food needs help now. In the longer term, reliable work, education and affordable services can make it easier to stay out of poverty. These measures need to fit together. A training place isn't much use if someone can't afford the bus fare or has nobody to look after their child. I'd start by asking where those practical barriers are, then design support around them. Otherwise, a promising programme can remain quite out of reach of the people it's meant to help.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー

    Do you think old(er) people have difficulties using some things that young people do not?

    Yes, sometimes, particularly when the design assumes knowledge a person hasn't had a chance to acquire. A younger user may know that a small symbol opens a menu, while someone used to physical buttons can see no clue about what to press. Small text can add another difficulty for anyone who struggles to read it. I wouldn't treat that as proof of lower ability. Give the person a clear explanation and time to practise, and the task may become quite manageable. Younger people can be just as lost with unfamiliar equipment, even if they're confident with a phone.

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What about cultural aspects? How can sports bring people from different countries closer together?

    Answer

    96 words

    Playing together gives people something to do before they have much to say to one another. In a mixed team, you can understand a pass, a missed chance or a shared joke even when conversation takes some effort. Then there are the moments around the game, when people ask about each other's lives or explain a local custom. Those small exchanges can make a country feel less like an unfamiliar name. It depends on how the sport is organised, though. Meeting as teammates creates different opportunities from simply treating the other side as a national rival.

    P3-485

    Sports

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What kind of puzzles improve people’s intelligence?

    Answer

    99 words

    I'd choose puzzles that make people explain and test an approach, such as a logic puzzle with several conditions. If your first answer fails, you have to work out which condition you missed instead of just trying the same thing again. But I'd be careful with the word 'intelligence'. Getting better at a particular puzzle doesn't, by itself, show a general improvement in thinking. I'd look for whether someone can use the same reasoning in a different problem. Puzzles can be enjoyable and give useful practice without needing to promise that every score reflects a change in overall ability.

    Shopping

    Which products are most consumed in your country? Why?
