    97 words

    If we're talking about regular household purchases in Japan, I'd start with food and drink: rice, vegetables, prepared meals and everyday drinks. These things need replacing continually, whereas a fridge may last for years. Food also takes a large share of household spending. The reasons are fairly ordinary: people need to eat every day, and something quick to prepare can fit around work or study. A person might buy ingredients when they have time to cook and pick up a ready-made meal on a busy evening. So daily need and convenience both help explain the repeated demand.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-504

    Study

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Can technology help people remember things better? How?

    Answer

    98 words

    Yes, especially by helping people recover information at the right moment. A calendar reminder can bring an appointment back to mind, and a photograph can give you a starting point for recalling an event. But storing something on a device isn't the same as remembering it yourself. I can save a note and still forget that the note exists. So the useful part is often the cue, the organisation or the chance to review it. If I wanted to learn something, I'd try recalling it before opening the saved version, so I could see what I actually remembered.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-507

    Study

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What is the most important practical skill in modern society?

    Answer

    96 words

    I'd choose clear communication, especially explaining a problem and checking that you've understood the reply. It helps at work, when dealing with a service and even when sharing a home. If you tell someone 'It doesn't work', they still have to discover what you tried and what happened. A more precise description gives them somewhere to begin. Listening matters just as much: repeating the main point in your own words can reveal a misunderstanding before it causes trouble. It's a skill you can keep improving, and it supports many of the more specialised skills people learn.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-513

    Teacher

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What role should the teacher have in the classroom?

    Answer

    95 words

    A teacher should make it possible for pupils to do work they couldn't yet manage alone. Sometimes that means explaining something clearly; sometimes it means setting a task and waiting while they struggle with it. I'd also expect the teacher to keep the discussion fair, so confident pupils don't take every turn. There's a judgement about timing here. If the teacher supplies each answer immediately, the class may look efficient while very little independent thinking happens. I think the role is to provide enough support, then gradually leave more of the work to the pupils.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-517

    Technology

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What’s the best invention in the past hundred years?

    Answer

    101 words

    I'd probably choose the transistor, although it's something most of us never notice. It was invented in 1947 and can act as an electronic switch or amplifier. Its development helped make computers and other electronic devices much smaller and more practical. What interests me is the distance between the little component and the things built with it: a person can send a message or work on a document without ever thinking about what's inside the machine. Other inventions have stronger claims if we use a different measure, but for its influence across so many everyday devices, I'd give it my vote.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-525

    Text Message

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Do you think modern technology has any negative influence on communication?

    Answer

    103 words

    Yes, it can make an exchange quicker than the understanding behind it. A short reply such as 'Fine' may be meant as simple agreement, but the other person might read irritation into it. Messages also make it easy to interrupt a conversation that's already happening in the room. Still, those problems depend on the way the technology is used. The same message can give someone time to express a difficult thought carefully. I'd say the main risk is assuming that because the words arrived immediately, their meaning arrived just as clearly. Sometimes a little more context, or a call, makes a considerable difference.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-526

    Text Message

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What do you think are some of the main differences between written communication and spoken communication?

    Answer

    96 words

    In speech, you can often see a puzzled face and change course straight away. If I say, 'I'll meet you there,' you can ask, 'Where exactly?' before we move on. Writing usually gives the sender more time to choose the words, and the reader can return to them later. But the writer has to supply context that a shared room or a tone of voice might otherwise provide. Messages can be quick exchanges too, of course. I'd say the main difference is how much the people involved can rely on immediate feedback and a shared situation.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-535

    Things

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What rules should be imposed to reduce noise pollution in the near future?

    Answer

    92 words

    I'd set clear quiet hours for building work and amplified outdoor music, with exceptions for urgent repairs. People should know when a noisy activity will end and whom to contact if it continues beyond the agreed limit. I'd also require organisations to maintain noisy equipment properly. The details would need to suit the area: a busy shopping street and a quiet residential road have different uses. Giving neighbours advance notice would help them plan, but notice alone shouldn't permit unlimited disturbance. The rules need a practical way to resolve complaints as well.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-538

    Time When Someone Apologised to You

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What do you think of those people who don’t apologise very often?

    Answer

    91 words

    I'd want to know what happens when they've actually hurt someone. A person may find the words awkward and try to put things right quietly; another may refuse to admit any responsibility. Those are quite different situations. Still, practical repair doesn't always tell the other person that their feelings have been understood. A simple 'I was wrong to do that' can remove a lot of uncertainty. So I wouldn't judge someone just by counting apologies, but I would pay attention to whether they acknowledge harm and change what they do afterwards.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-539

    Traditional Products

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What different types of traditional products are produced in your country?

    Answer

    91 words

    Japan produces pottery, lacquered wooden bowls and trays, woven or dyed cloth, and handmade paper, among other traditional products. Different regions have their own materials and ways of making things, so even an ordinary cup can have a recognisable local character. Some pieces are intended for special occasions, while others are useful every day. I particularly like that second group. A bowl used for breakfast can keep a traditional skill present in an ordinary household routine; you don't have to treat every carefully made object as something too precious to touch.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-557

    Transport

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do you think more and more people prefer to travel by plane?

    Answer

    118 words

    I think speed is the main attraction, especially over long distances. One possible reason for the shift towards flying is a wider choice of affordable direct services, which could bring it within reach of people who wouldn't have considered it before. If someone has only a few days away from work, spending most of one day on a train can make the trip difficult. A flight may leave more time at the destination. The comparison changes for shorter journeys, though, once you include travelling to the airport and waiting there. So I can see why more people might choose planes when distance and limited time matter, without assuming flying is the quickest or best choice for every trip.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-559

    Travel

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Why do some people prefer to travel abroad rather than travel in their own country?

    Answer

    100 words

    For some people, going abroad makes the break feel more complete. Even buying breakfast or finding the right platform may involve unfamiliar words and habits, so they pay closer attention than they would at home. There may also be a particular landscape, building or way of life they want to experience. Others are visiting friends or relatives, which gives the journey a different purpose. I don't think the preference necessarily means they dislike their own country. They may simply want a change from what they already know, and a little distance can make familiar things interesting again when they return.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-577

    TV

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How popular is watching television in your country?

    Answer

    94 words

    Television is still popular in Japan, especially among older viewers, but I'd separate following a programme from watching it as it's broadcast. Younger people often spend more time with online video, and someone who follows a television series may watch it later on a phone. That changes the place it has in the day. For one household, the evening news might be a regular shared event; for another, each person chooses something at a different time. So it's still widely watched, although the idea of everybody gathering around one set doesn't describe every home.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-583

    Vegetables

    問題へ戻る ↗

    How do people feel when they eat vegetables that they grew on their own?

    Answer

    94 words

    They may feel proud, relieved and quite protective of the result. Even a small crop represents weeks of watering and waiting. A handful of beans can seem ordinary in a shop, but it feels different when you've watched them grow. People may notice the taste and shape more carefully, or enjoy sharing the vegetables and telling someone where they came from. A slightly crooked carrot might even become a favourite. I think part of the pleasure is that the meal has a story they took part in, from the first shoots to the plate.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-586

    Weather

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Describe the seasons in your country

    Answer

    96 words

    Across much of Japan, spring gradually warms up, summer is hot and humid, autumn turns cooler and winter brings the cold back. There's often a rainy spell in early summer as well. The pattern varies a great deal by region: northern areas can have severe, snowy winters, while Okinawa stays much milder. I think the changes are easiest to notice in ordinary routines: when you can leave a window open, which clothes you reach for, and whether an evening walk feels inviting. So there are four recognisable seasons, but one description can't capture the weather everywhere.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    P3-590

    Work

    問題へ戻る ↗

    What’s the difference between white-collar and blue-collar jobs?

    Answer

    93 words

    They're broad labels for different kinds of work. White-collar jobs usually involve office, administrative or professional tasks, while blue-collar jobs tend to involve making, building, maintaining or moving physical things. But the boundary is far from exact. An engineer may spend time at a desk and on a factory floor, and a skilled repair worker may solve very complex problems. I wouldn't use the labels as a scale of intelligence or worth. They can describe the setting and main activity, but they tell you much less about a person's skill, pay or responsibility.

    Writing Task 2

    W2-0001

    Health Services & Access

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that a larger share of public health spending should go towards preventing illness. Others believe that treating people who are already ill must remain the main priority.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    335 words

    Health services must deal with two kinds of need: the illness that has arrived and the illness that might still be prevented. Both deserve public money. I favour increasing the share spent on effective prevention, provided that essential treatment remains available to people who need it now.

    The case for giving treatment priority begins with an immediate obligation. A person waiting for an operation cannot postpone their pain until a healthier society has been built. Hospitals also need trained staff, equipment and reliable services, which cannot be assembled whenever an emergency happens. If prevention were funded by removing necessary care, the public would be asked to accept a certain loss in return for a possible future benefit. That would be difficult to justify, especially for people who could not buy treatment privately.

    However, a health service that deals only with illness after it appears leaves much of its work unfinished. Measures such as providing clean drinking water or making routine vaccinations accessible can address risks before a hospital bed is required. Prevention has an awkward disadvantage in a budget discussion: when it works, the event it prevented is absent. A ward full of patients is visible; people who never needed the ward are harder to count. This difference in visibility should not determine the value of the spending.

    The practical question is therefore which preventive measures offer worthwhile benefits, and how they can be introduced without weakening essential care. A gradual shift towards well-supported programmes is more defensible than a fixed rule that prevention must always receive the largest share. Prevention can reduce risks without guaranteeing that everyone will stay well. Falling ill does not, by itself, show irresponsible choices or remove our responsibility to those affected.

    I would consequently protect a dependable treatment service while directing additional resources towards effective prevention. The two approaches should be judged by their contribution to health, including present suffering and future need. A successful system should help people recover, and give fewer people a reason to enter it.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0039

    Healthy Lifestyles & Sleep

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Night-time work should be limited to essential services, even when other businesses would benefit from operating around the clock.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    344 words

    Keeping a business open throughout the night may be convenient for its customers, but the night does not disappear for the people working there. I agree that routine night work should be reduced. However, I would not limit it to a rigid list of essential services, because a rule intended to protect workers also needs to recognise their different circumstances.

    There is a strong reason to place limits on businesses that operate around the clock simply to offer greater convenience. Employees still need time to sleep, see their families and take part in ordinary social life. A shop may gain a few extra hours of trade while a worker loses the hours in which their family and friends are free. Where the same service could reasonably be provided during the day, employers should have to justify the burden of keeping it available at night. Customer demand alone is an incomplete justification.

    However, essential and non-essential work cannot always be separated neatly. A theatre is not an emergency service, yet technicians may need to work past midnight to finish safely after a late performance. A strict ban could make some worthwhile evening events impractical. Some workers may also prefer evening or night hours because these fit their responsibilities. Their preference should count, although it must be a real choice rather than an agreement extracted by the threat of losing a job.

    A better policy would combine restrictions with enforceable working conditions. Employers should provide predictable schedules, adequate breaks and a reasonable way to move away from night work. Services whose interruption would cause serious harm, such as emergency care, would plainly need to continue. Other businesses should demonstrate a worthwhile purpose and suitable arrangements for staff, rather than treating continuous opening as the natural state of affairs.

    I therefore support a presumption against unnecessary night work, not an absolute ban outside essential services. The aim should be to make useful activity possible while leaving workers enough of a life beyond it. Useful activity can continue after dark without treating uninterrupted trade as a public need.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0045

    Medical Advances & Human Health

    問題へ戻る ↗

    The results of medical research paid for by public money should be made freely available to the public.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    328 words

    Publicly funded medical research is undertaken partly for the benefit of people who may never enter a laboratory. I strongly agree that its results should be freely available. This should mean access to findings and the methods needed to assess them, while preserving the confidentiality owed to research participants.

    The strongest reason for open access is that useful knowledge can travel beyond the team that produced it. A doctor in a small hospital, a researcher in another field or a patient trying to understand a condition may each find something valuable in the same report. Their ability to read it should not depend entirely on the subscriptions their organisation can afford. Wider access also allows others to examine the reasoning, identify weaknesses and attempt to repeat the work. Public payment should therefore support public scrutiny as well as public benefit.

    However, availability alone does not make a result understandable. An article can be free to download and still be difficult to enter. A technical paper should be accompanied, where possible, by a clear account of what was studied, what was found and what remains uncertain. Such an explanation must retain the limits of the evidence. Turning a tentative finding into a confident promise would make the language easier at the expense of the meaning.

    There are also legitimate boundaries around what is released. Publishing research results does not require publishing identifiable medical records. Information that could expose a participant should remain protected, and sharing detailed data may require controlled arrangements. These safeguards concern the treatment of people, rather than a general reason to keep conclusions behind a payment barrier. The cost of preparing and distributing accessible reports should be included in the research budget.

    I would therefore make free publication of results a normal condition of public research funding. Both encouraging and disappointing findings deserve a place in that record. The community should be able to see what its investment established, including the questions it did not settle.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0053

    Medical Advances & Human Health

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some healthcare systems now allow patients to view their medical records and test information directly, rather than receiving all information through a medical professional.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    324 words

    Allowing patients to read their own medical records is, on balance, a positive development. Information about a person’s care should help that person participate in it. Direct access can make this possible, although access to a result and understanding a result are two different achievements.

    One benefit is that patients can check information at a time when they are able to concentrate. During an appointment, an unfamiliar term may arrive just as they are trying to remember the answer to an earlier question. Afterwards, a written record allows them to return to the explanation, prepare questions and keep track of what has been agreed. They may also notice an incorrect detail about their own history. In this sense, the record becomes something that can be checked together, rather than something the patient must remember from a single conversation.

    The main difficulty is interpretation. A result can appear precise on a screen while leaving its significance unclear. A patient might be alarmed by an unfamiliar label or reassured by one number without understanding the wider picture. Simply releasing more information does not remove this problem. It may move the uncertainty from the consulting room to the kitchen table, where there is nobody immediately available to answer.

    For this reason, direct access should come with clear explanations and a practical route to professional advice. Records should distinguish confirmed findings from possibilities under investigation, and patients should know when and how they will receive further guidance. Privacy also matters: a convenient system is of limited value if people cannot trust it to protect sensitive information. Those who do not use digital services should retain another way to obtain their records.

    These requirements support direct access rather than undermine it. The aim is a more informed partnership, with patients able to see information and professionals helping them understand its relevance. Opening the record is a useful first step; the next is to make the conversation around it easier.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0070

    Character, Values & Behaviour

    問題へ戻る ↗

    In some communities, people are becoming more willing to question the judgement of authority figures instead of accepting it automatically.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    315 words

    A judgement can be accepted because its reasons are sound, or because the person giving it is difficult to question. These may look alike in a quiet meeting, but they are different kinds of agreement. I regard a growing willingness to question authority as a positive development when it makes decisions more open to explanation and correction.

    Questions can reveal information that an authority figure has missed. A manager may design a sensible timetable without knowing that one stage of the work regularly takes longer than expected. An employee who asks how the schedule will operate is contributing knowledge, even if the question initially sounds like an objection. Similarly, asking a teacher to explain a conclusion can help a student understand both the answer and the route to it. Respect need not require everyone else to stop thinking.

    This willingness also changes the responsibilities of those with authority. A decision that affects other people should normally come with reasons they can examine. Requiring an explanation can expose inconsistent treatment or an assumption that has survived simply because nobody has named it. Even when the original judgement remains unchanged, an open exchange may give people a better basis for trusting it.

    Questioning can nevertheless become unhelpful if it means treating every answer as evidence of dishonesty. Expertise matters, and a person who challenges a conclusion should be willing to consider the reply. There are also moments, such as an immediate safety emergency, when following a clear instruction must precede a fuller discussion. These limits concern how and when questions are raised; they do not establish that authority should be beyond examination.

    Overall, I welcome the change. Its value lies in the possibility of better shared decisions, rather than in the number of objections voiced. A healthy relationship with authority leaves room for someone to ask why, and for both sides to learn something from the answer.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0078

    Character, Values & Behaviour

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some organisations use references describing an applicant's character, alongside evidence of qualifications or practical ability.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of using character references in this way?

    Answer

    313 words

    A qualification can show that someone has learnt a subject, while a practical test can show what they can do on a particular afternoon. Neither necessarily reveals how they treat colleagues over several difficult months. Character references can help fill that gap, although their value depends heavily on whose account is being offered and what supports it.

    Their main advantage is access to behaviour that an interview rarely captures. A former supervisor might describe how an applicant admitted an error, shared an unpopular task or responded when a deadline became unrealistic. Such details can matter in work requiring trust and cooperation. They also give an applicant an opportunity to demonstrate strengths that formal qualifications overlook. Someone with modest examination results may nevertheless be exceptionally reliable when other people depend on them.

    The difficulty begins when an account of conduct becomes a certificate of personal goodness. A friendly referee may offer praise without having observed anything relevant; a hostile one may turn a disagreement into a permanent defect of character. Applicants with influential contacts can obtain impressive letters, whereas equally capable people who have moved frequently or taken time away from work may struggle to find a suitable referee. The document then measures access to recommendation as much as suitability for the job.

    There is a further risk of treating behaviour in one setting as a prediction for every setting. A person who was quiet in a tightly controlled workplace might contribute readily in a team that welcomes questions. References should therefore identify the circumstances and the referee's relationship with the applicant, allowing the organisation to judge how far the account applies.

    Used alongside qualifications and direct assessment, a specific, relevant reference can improve a decision. Used as an unquestionable verdict, it can give personal preference an official appearance. Organisations gain most when they ask for observed examples and retain responsibility for interpreting them.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0083

    Emotions, Well-being & Stress

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some employers pay for confidential counselling that their employees can use voluntarily, without telling their manager why they need it.

    Do the advantages of providing this service outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    325 words

    An employee may be willing to ask for help yet unwilling to explain a private difficulty to the person who allocates their work. Employer-funded confidential counselling offers a separate route. I believe its advantages generally outweigh its disadvantages, provided that appointments are accessible and the service supplements efforts to improve working conditions.

    Paying for the service removes one possible obstacle to seeking support. The employee can discuss a concern with someone whose role is to listen and help them consider it, without first making a case to a manager. Voluntary use also leaves room for different preferences: an offer need not become another workplace instruction. For someone struggling to decide what help they need, having an accessible starting point can itself be valuable. Any benefit to attendance or productivity should be treated as an additional gain rather than the sole reason for offering care.

    There are costs, however, and a confidential service can still be difficult to use. Paying for appointments may leave a smaller employer with less money for other forms of support. Employees may also struggle to find time to attend without leaving urgent work to colleagues. No private explanation is required, but the practical obstacle remains. Flexible appointment times and a reasonable allowance for attendance can help ensure that the offer is usable.

    The other danger is organisational complacency. A manager might respond to repeated complaints about excessive workloads by pointing towards counselling, leaving the workload untouched. Support for an individual cannot by itself repair every condition affecting that individual. Employers still need to listen to concerns about schedules, staffing and conduct at work.

    These disadvantages are substantial but can largely be addressed through the design of the service and responsible management. Against them stands a continuing opportunity for employees to seek help without paying or disclosing their reasons to a supervisor. Where that opportunity is real, the expense is justified; the counselling room should be one part of a considerate workplace.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0107

    Success, Talent & Motivation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some adults abandon goals that were once important to them before making much progress towards achieving them.

    Why does this happen? What could help people sustain their commitment to a goal?

    Answer

    334 words

    A goal can occupy a large place in someone's imagination while finding no place at all in their week. Adults sometimes abandon important ambitions because the connection between the desired result and daily action remains weak. Competing responsibilities and a changing sense of what matters can weaken it further.

    At the beginning, the destination is usually easier to picture than the journey. Someone may imagine speaking another language comfortably without having considered the repeated practice required after a tiring day. Early efforts then produce much less visible change than expected. If progress is judged only against the finished achievement, each incomplete attempt can look like evidence of failure. Work, caring duties and financial pressures may also leave less time or energy than the original plan assumed. The goal survives in principle while its opportunities gradually disappear.

    Commitment is easier to sustain when the next action is small enough to fit the person's actual circumstances. Instead of promising to become fluent, a learner could set aside a short, regular period to explain one familiar subject and return to it later. Keeping a record of what has become easier makes modest progress visible. A class, practice partner or agreed appointment can provide both continuity and someone with whom to discuss difficulties. These arrangements should support action without turning every missed session into a personal judgement.

    It is equally useful to revisit why the goal was chosen. An ambition adopted to please another person may lose its force once the initial encouragement fades. Even a deeply personal aim may need a slower timetable or a different route after circumstances change. Reviewing the purpose allows a person to preserve what still matters while adjusting an unrealistic method.

    Sustained effort therefore requires a workable rhythm, proportionate evidence of progress and a reason that remains persuasive. Occasionally, review will show that a goal deserves to be abandoned. The aim should be to help people continue thoughtfully, with enough freedom to recognise when their lives have made another direction more worthwhile.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0122

    Families, Parenting & Generations

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people believe that young children are best cared for by relatives when their parents are working. Others think that professional childcare services offer greater benefits.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    336 words

    When parents leave for work, the important question is what happens during the hours before they return. Relatives may offer familiar, flexible care, while professional services can provide organised activities and dependable arrangements. Both views have merit. My preference is for professional childcare where it is suitable and affordable, with relatives retaining a valuable supporting role.

    The strongest argument for family care is continuity. A grandparent or other relative may already know a child's routines, favourite games and particular worries. The child does not have to establish every relationship afresh, and a late meeting need not create an entirely unfamiliar evening. Care within a family can also bring generations into regular contact. An ordinary afternoon spent preparing food or listening to a story may have a value that cannot be reduced to a timetable of educational activities.

    However, familiarity does not settle every practical question. A willing relative may have health concerns, other commitments or different ideas about discipline. If an informal arrangement grows into a full working week without discussion, affection can acquire a considerable workload. Parents should therefore consider the carer's wishes and capacity as carefully as the child's comfort.

    Professional childcare offers a different set of advantages. A well-run service can organise play with other children, provide appropriate materials and arrange cover when a member of staff is absent. Responsibilities can be made explicit, giving parents a clearer basis for raising concerns. Yet these benefits depend on the actual service: a professional label alone says little about the attention a particular child receives. Fees, travelling time and fixed opening hours may also make an otherwise attractive option impractical.

    I favour professional care as the main arrangement when its quality and availability can be established, because regular work requires a service that is deliberately organised to continue. Family involvement can then remain flexible and welcome. Where such a service is unavailable, a carefully agreed family arrangement may be better. The child's daily experience and the carer's ability to sustain it should decide the matter.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0150

    Friendship & Community

    問題へ戻る ↗

    People who move into a new neighbourhood should make an effort to participate in its community life, even if they expect to live there only temporarily.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    327 words

    Expecting to leave a neighbourhood does not prevent someone from affecting it while they live there. A temporary resident uses shared spaces, encounters neighbours and contributes to the character of the place through everyday behaviour. I therefore agree that newcomers should make an effort to participate, although that effort should be proportionate to their circumstances and length of stay.

    Small forms of involvement can make daily life easier for everyone. Introducing oneself, learning how shared areas are used and attending an occasional residents' meeting can prevent misunderstandings that would otherwise become unnecessary disputes. A newcomer who knows whom to ask about a broken gate is less isolated and better able to help resolve the problem. These benefits can arise during a short tenancy; they do not wait for someone to become a permanent resident.

    Participation also gives temporary residents a voice. People who are passing through may notice obstacles that established neighbours have learnt to accept, such as confusing notices or activities that are difficult to join. Listening to them can make a community more accessible to its next arrivals. In return, newcomers gain a clearer understanding of why local arrangements exist, rather than judging them entirely from the outside.

    The word 'should', however, needs sensible limits. A person working long shifts or caring for someone at home may have little time for organised events. Others may wish to keep their private lives separate from their immediate surroundings. Community life should offer ways to contribute at different levels, from helping with one practical task to simply being a considerate neighbour. For a short-term tenant, helping at one event may be more realistic than joining an organising committee.

    I therefore support reasonable engagement that leaves room for privacy and limited time. Temporary residents can take an interest, offer modest help and leave shared spaces in good order. Even if they never see the eventual result of every contribution, the next person will live with what they leave behind.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0176

    Social Customs, Manners & Cooperation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    In some communities, carefully planned visits with formal hospitality are becoming less common, while brief and informal meetings are becoming more usual.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    320 words

    A visit becomes difficult to arrange when it seems to require a spotless house, a carefully prepared meal and an afternoon that nobody possesses. The growing preference for brief, informal meetings can remove some of these barriers. I regard this as a broadly positive development, although communities would lose something if every encounter became hurried.

    Informality lowers the cost of keeping in touch. Friends can meet for a walk or share a cup of tea without one household undertaking all the preparation. Someone with limited money, space or energy can invite another person into their day without feeling obliged to provide an impressive occasion. When the standard of hospitality becomes easier to meet, contact may become more frequent. A modest invitation is often easier to accept as well as to offer.

    Brief meetings can also fit around the changing pattern of people's lives. Two neighbours may have time for a conversation after collecting their children even when their weekends never coincide. Such encounters allow a relationship to continue through busy periods, preserving the familiarity from which a longer conversation may later grow. Their value lies partly in their ordinary place in the week.

    Formal visits nevertheless offer more than elaborate food. Setting aside time tells a guest that their company matters, and preparation can express care in a form that words do not quite supply. Longer visits may allow difficult subjects to emerge gradually, after the cheerful answer to the first question has worn thin. If informal contact always occurs between other commitments, people can remain well acquainted with one another's schedules while knowing very little about one another's concerns.

    The change is beneficial when it expands the ways people can meet. Everyday contact need not wait until someone can host an occasion, but occasional unhurried visits still deserve a place. Communities gain most when hospitality becomes flexible enough to welcome more people and patient enough to let them stay.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0191

    Diet, Food Choices & Public Policy

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some public institutions involve the people who use their catering services in planning future menus.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of involving users in these decisions?

    Answer

    338 words

    The people who plan a public institution's menu may know its budget precisely while knowing rather less about what diners leave on their plates. Involving users can bring those two kinds of information together. It offers practical benefits, but also creates difficulties when preferences conflict or participation is treated as a promise to satisfy everyone.

    Users can explain problems that sales figures or a list of ingredients do not reveal. A dish may be unpopular because its portion is too large, its sauce too strong or it is unavailable at a convenient time. Discussing these details allows catering staff to make more useful changes than simply removing the least popular item. People with dietary requirements can also describe whether they have a genuine choice across the week, rather than one technically suitable meal repeated indefinitely. Better understanding may improve satisfaction and reduce avoidable waste.

    There is an educational advantage as well. Planning a menu makes visible the choices behind a meal: ingredients must be bought, preparation fitted into the working day and different needs accommodated within limited funds. Users who discuss those constraints may offer more workable suggestions and understand why every request cannot be accepted.

    However, participation consumes staff time and can give disproportionate influence to the most vocal users. A meeting dominated by confident regular customers may overlook people who rarely speak or cannot attend. Popularity is also an incomplete basis for a public menu. Institutions must retain responsibility for food safety, appropriate nutritional standards and fair access, even when the most popular proposal would make these harder to achieve. An extensive consultation followed by no visible change can leave users more disappointed than before.

    The arrangement therefore works best as a continuing exchange of information with clear decision-making responsibilities. Brief surveys, small tasting sessions and targeted conversations can bring different voices into the process. Staff should explain which suggestions they adopted and why others were impractical. Diners need a meaningful part in the conversation, together with an honest account of what the kitchen can provide.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0212

    Food Production, Farming & Food Security

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some governments offer financial support to people who want to start farming but do not already own agricultural land.

    Do the advantages of offering this support outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    334 words

    A person may know how to grow crops yet have nowhere secure to plant them. Financial support for people without agricultural property can open the occupation to capable newcomers. I believe this advantage outweighs the risks, as long as assistance creates a workable route into farming instead of merely making an initial payment easier.

    The chief benefit is a wider pool of possible farmers. Someone may have relevant skills and a sound plan yet lack the savings to secure land, equipment and materials at the same time. Support can help that person begin, bringing experience gained outside an existing family farm into the sector. New entrants might also choose crops or methods suited to a local opportunity that current businesses have overlooked. Such contributions become possible when access depends less heavily on inherited property or accumulated wealth.

    Nevertheless, starting a farm and sustaining it are different tasks. A grant may cover equipment while leaving the recipient with an insecure lease or running costs that the business cannot meet. Public funds would then have purchased an encouraging beginning followed by an expensive failure. Support may also benefit landowners more than applicants if owners respond to increased purchasing power by demanding higher rents. Neither risk disappears simply because the intended recipient is enthusiastic.

    These problems favour staged assistance. Applicants should be able to demonstrate relevant knowledge, realistic costs and a sufficiently stable arrangement for using the land. Part of the funding could become available as agreed steps are completed, with practical advice available when the plan needs revision. This approach would still involve failures, but it would limit the amount committed before serious difficulties became apparent.

    On balance, leaving capable people unable to enter farming despite a viable plan carries a lasting cost in lost opportunity. The disadvantages of support concern how much public money is exposed and what it actually secures. Carefully designed assistance can control those risks while giving capable people a fair chance to establish a farm that continues beyond its first season.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0237

    Cooking, Food Education & Eating Out

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people enjoy watching cooking programmes but rarely prepare the dishes or practise the skills shown.

    Why can cooking be appealing as entertainment? How might these programmes still influence people's relationship with food?

    Answer

    336 words

    A viewer can enjoy seeing a complicated dinner emerge from a collection of ingredients without wanting to reproduce it on a Tuesday evening. Cooking programmes offer stories, spectacle and companionship as well as instruction. Their influence on food can therefore extend beyond the number of recipes viewers actually attempt.

    Part of the appeal is the visible movement towards a finished result. Ingredients are chosen, something is mixed or heated, a difficulty appears and eventually a dish reaches the table. Competition adds uncertainty about who will succeed, while a familiar presenter can make even routine preparation enjoyable to watch. The viewer receives the satisfying conclusion without having to shop, clear a work surface or wash a single pan. For someone tired after work, that distance from the effort may be part of the attraction.

    Programmes can also provide access to places and experiences that viewers cannot easily encounter themselves. A family recipe or a meal prepared in an unfamiliar region can connect food with memory, landscape and social life. People may watch out of curiosity about those connections rather than with a notebook open. Enjoying such a programme need not be an unsuccessful attempt to learn cooking.

    Even without practice, viewing can change what people notice. They may become more curious about an ingredient, recognise the work involved in a restaurant meal or ask how a familiar product is made. A small choice at the shops may reflect that interest, although it is less visible than a completed recipe. At the same time, polished programmes can make everyday meals appear disappointingly simple. If every dish arrives perfectly arranged and every mistake is neatly resolved, viewers may underestimate the time, expense and untidiness involved in ordinary cooking.

    The influence is therefore mixed. These programmes can deepen curiosity and appreciation, or encourage expectations that an everyday kitchen cannot reasonably fulfil. Their most useful effect may sometimes be a more attentive eater: someone who tastes a meal with a new question in mind, even if another person has cooked it.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0246

    Food Trade, Shopping & Waste

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that the government should regulate the prices of essential foods. Others believe that retailers should be free to set prices in response to supply and demand.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    327 words

    Essential food is an unusual purchase: households can change what they eat, but they cannot indefinitely postpone eating. This gives governments a strong reason to protect affordability. Even so, I favour allowing prices to reflect supply and demand, combined with targeted help and scrutiny of unfair practices, rather than routine government control of retail prices.

    Those who support regulation are concerned with the immediate position of the shopper. When the price of basic food rises sharply, a household with very little spare income cannot necessarily absorb the increase. A regulated price can give people greater certainty and prevent sellers from taking advantage of an urgent need. The argument is particularly persuasive when customers have few alternative shops. In those circumstances, describing a price as freely chosen by a retailer tells us little about how freely the customer can refuse it. Regulation promises a limit to that imbalance.

    Supporters of flexible prices look further along the route by which food reaches the shelf. Retailers must cover what they pay suppliers, together with transport, storage and other costs. If a price limit falls below those costs, a shop may reduce the quantity it stocks or stop selling the item. The cheap price then remains on the label while the food disappears. Higher prices can also encourage suppliers to bring additional goods to an area where they are scarce. This response is valuable, although it does not excuse exploitation or guarantee that poorer customers can afford the result.

    My view is that affordability and availability must be addressed together. Direct assistance to households can help them buy essentials while allowing suppliers to respond to changing costs. Authorities should also examine misleading pricing and obstacles to competition. Temporary price measures may be justified in an exceptional disruption, but they need a clear account of how supply will be maintained. A policy should ultimately be judged by whether people can obtain sufficient food, including those whose budgets leave them the fewest choices.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0272

    Fashion, Clothing & Identity

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Young people should be taught basic clothing repair skills so that they can maintain the things they wear instead of always replacing them.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    322 words

    I strongly agree that young people should learn basic clothing repair. A loose button or a small opening in a seam need not end the useful life of a garment, yet it can do so when its owner has no idea how to begin. A modest amount of practical teaching would give them another option.

    The most immediate benefit is control over ordinary problems. Learning to thread a needle, secure a button and close a simple tear can save both money and the inconvenience of replacing something that otherwise fits well. The lesson should involve an actual repair: examining the damage, choosing suitable thread, making a few stitches and checking whether the fabric still moves comfortably. Each step answers a visible need. A pupil who completes it has more than a description of sewing; they have a small procedure they can try again when a similar problem appears.

    Repair can also change how clothing is valued. Looking closely at a seam reveals something about how a garment is made and why one kind of damage is easy to mend while another is difficult. That attention may encourage more careful buying and maintenance. It can also preserve possessions with personal significance, such as a jacket that has accompanied someone through several winters. The repair need not be invisible to be worthwhile. Teaching should make room for a neat practical mend and for a deliberately visible patch, allowing young people to choose the appearance they want.

    These skills should be taught as a useful foundation, with accessible tools and suitable alternatives for pupils who find fine handwork difficult. Complicated alterations or repairs to badly worn fabric can remain work for someone more experienced. Basic instruction does not oblige young people to preserve every item indefinitely; it enables them to judge which items can reasonably be kept. A few well-designed lessons, followed by chances to practise, would be a worthwhile part of their practical education.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0290

    Shopping, Advertising & Consumer Choices

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some retailers now let customers explore a product through interactive digital demonstrations before visiting a shop or placing an order.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    318 words

    Being able to turn a product around on a screen or explore its controls before ordering it is a useful extension of shopping. I consider interactive digital demonstrations a positive development because they can answer practical questions before a customer commits time or money. Their value is greatest when the demonstration makes its own limits clear.

    Consider someone choosing a desk for a small room. A demonstration might show how its drawers open, where cables pass and how much space a chair needs beneath it. The customer can inspect the same detail several times without feeling hurried, compare alternatives and arrive at a shop with more precise questions. Someone who lives far from the retailer may be able to rule out an unsuitable product without making the journey. This is more informative than a carefully chosen photograph, provided the dimensions and functions shown accurately represent the item being sold.

    The screen nevertheless offers a particular kind of evidence. It may display the shape of a chair beautifully while revealing little about how the seat feels after an hour. Movement can look smooth because the animation was designed to be smooth. Customers may overlook these differences when a demonstration is convincing, and retailers have an obvious interest in presenting the most attractive version of the experience. Clear measurements, honest descriptions of what is simulated and opportunities to inspect or return the physical product remain important. The demonstration should sit beside those sources of information.

    There is also a question of access. An interactive feature should not remove ordinary photographs, written specifications or assistance for customers who cannot easily use it. With those alternatives available, the overall gain is persuasive: shoppers have an additional way to investigate a purchase, and shops can spend more time answering questions that genuinely require human help. The best demonstrations leave customers better prepared to judge the product once it is in front of them.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0313

    Ownership, Sharing & Material Consumption

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some companies allow customers to pay a regular fee to use household equipment instead of buying it outright.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of using equipment through a subscription?

    Answer

    325 words

    A household needs clean clothes long before it has necessarily saved enough to buy a washing machine. Subscribing to equipment can bridge that gap by spreading payment over the period of use. The arrangement offers flexibility and possible relief from maintenance, but creates continuing costs and dependence on the provider.

    Avoiding a large initial payment is particularly useful when several household needs arise together. Someone moving into an unfurnished home may be able to use essential equipment immediately while retaining money for rent and other expenses. If the subscription includes repairs or replacement, the customer also has a clear place to turn when a machine fails. For a person expecting to move again soon, returning an appliance at the end of the agreement may be easier than transporting or selling it. The service can make practical sense even where outright ownership would be cheaper over a longer period.

    That longer period is the main financial disadvantage. A small monthly fee can become a substantial total, and after paying it for years the customer may still own nothing. Charges for damage, delivery or early cancellation can alter the apparent price further. These details matter especially when the equipment is essential: a household cannot simply stop washing clothes while it disputes a bill. Its convenience also depends on the provider keeping promises. A repair service has limited value if appointments are difficult to obtain, and a replacement offered without a clear timescale leaves the original problem unresolved.

    Subscriptions are therefore most attractive when the expected period of use is limited, the total cost is understandable and maintenance is genuinely included. Customers planning to keep reliable equipment for many years may gain more from buying it. Providers should make repair responsibilities and exit terms clear enough for that comparison to be possible. The useful question is how the arrangement will serve the household throughout its likely use of the equipment, including the day when the machine stops working.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0337

    Housing & Accommodation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some local authorities impose additional charges on homes that remain empty for long periods in areas where housing is in high demand.

    Do the advantages of these charges outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    333 words

    In an area where many people need a home, a usable property left empty for years represents a missed opportunity. Additional charges can give its owner a reason to bring it back into use. I believe the benefits outweigh the disadvantages when the policy targets avoidable long-term vacancy and allows reasonable time to resolve genuine obstacles.

    The principal advantage is the possibility of making existing accommodation available without waiting for construction. An owner who has been content to leave a property unused may decide to rent, sell or renovate it once keeping it empty carries a recurring cost. If that leads to an occupied home, the benefit reaches beyond the new household: a street gains another resident, and neighbours have someone to contact about the property. Income from the charge could also help an authority identify vacant buildings and support their return to use. These are practical gains in places where demand is already high.

    However, an empty building is not always a home waiting only for an owner to change their mind. Extensive repairs, a disputed ownership arrangement or difficulty securing funds may prevent occupation. A charge can make the last problem worse by taking money that might otherwise help complete the work. Authorities must also distinguish genuine vacancy from occasional absence, which requires administration and a fair process for correcting mistakes. Poorly designed rules may encourage superficial signs of occupation while leaving the underlying shortage untouched.

    These disadvantages justify careful eligibility rules and review, rather than abandoning the approach. A period of notice, evidence-based exceptions and advice about available routes to repair or letting can make the charge more effective. Its contribution will remain limited by the number of suitable empty properties; new housing and wider access measures may still be needed. Within that limit, encouraging owners to use existing homes offers a substantial benefit relative to the manageable administrative burden. The strongest policy is one under which fewer properties eventually incur the charge because more of them are lived in.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0347

    Urban Development & Public Spaces

    問題へ戻る ↗

    City centres in different countries sometimes look very similar, with the same kinds of buildings and public spaces.

    Why does this happen? What effects can it have on people's experience of a city?

    Answer

    322 words

    A visitor may arrive in a new country and find a city centre that already feels familiar: glass offices, a broad paved square and shops arranged in a recognisable pattern. Similarity can arise from shared commercial pressures and design choices. It makes some aspects of urban life easier to navigate, while risking the loss of qualities that make a place distinctive.

    Developers and planners often face comparable demands for office space, transport access and places to shop. Reusing a familiar building type can make a project easier to cost and explain to investors. International retailers may also seek premises that suit an established layout, encouraging similar street fronts wherever they operate. Design ideas circulate between cities, and a public space admired in one location can become a model elsewhere. Each individual decision may seem reasonable; together they can produce a centre that resembles many others, even without anyone intending to erase its identity.

    For users, some familiarity is welcome. A visitor can find an entrance, recognise a pedestrian area or understand how to move between shops without learning everything from the beginning. Residents may benefit from well-planned spaces that adopt useful ideas from elsewhere. Yet a layout cannot be separated entirely from its setting. An open square that is pleasant in one climate may offer too little shelter in another. Replacing small streets and distinctive meeting places with a standard arrangement can also disrupt the routes, memories and habits through which residents know their city. The centre may become easier to read in general and less expressive of this particular place.

    The effects therefore depend on what is shared and what is displaced. Cities can borrow accessible layouts and effective building methods while adapting them to local weather, existing streets and patterns of use. Retaining familiar landmarks and room for local businesses gives both residents and visitors reasons to notice their surroundings. Useful design travels well when it is reconsidered on arrival.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0379

    Rural Life & Regional Development

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people favour concentrating investment in a few regional towns so that they become centres of growth. Others favour spreading investment across many smaller settlements.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    336 words

    Regional investment has to reach people whose homes are spread across a wide area. Concentrating it in a few towns can create strong services and employment centres; distributing it among smaller settlements can keep opportunity closer to where people already live. I favour a connected network of regional centres, with essential local investment protected rather than left to whatever funding remains.

    The case for concentration rests on what a substantial project can achieve. A training centre, for example, needs equipment, instructors and enough learners to sustain a useful range of courses. Bringing those resources together may offer residents more than several smaller projects with limited provision. Businesses can benefit from being near suppliers and a larger pool of workers, allowing a town to become a practical base for the surrounding region. The weakness appears when the centre is easy to reach only for people who already live there. A place can be labelled a regional hub while remaining distant from much of its intended population.

    Those who favour wider distribution are responding to that distance. Investment in reliable internet connections, small business premises or a local meeting space can support activity within villages and smaller towns. Residents may then find work or services without leaving their community, and local decisions can reflect needs that a central plan overlooks. However, spreading a fixed budget creates difficult choices about scale. If too many schemes receive too little to become usable, the appearance of fairness can conceal a collection of unfinished promises. Distribution needs a clear purpose for each project.

    My preference combines concentration where scale is necessary with local provision where proximity matters. Larger specialist facilities can serve several settlements if transport and access are planned alongside them. Basic connections, shared spaces and suitable support for local enterprise should reach the smaller places themselves. This requires cooperation between towns and their surrounding communities, including an honest assessment of travel time. A regional centre earns its role through the opportunities people can actually reach from their own front doors.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0387

    Daily Routines, Domestic Work & Living Arrangements

    問題へ戻る ↗

    All adults who share a home should be able to carry out basic domestic tasks, regardless of how the work is normally divided.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    331 words

    Sharing domestic work does not require everyone to perform the same tasks every day. It is nevertheless sensible for adults who share a home to learn enough basic work to manage when the usual arrangement changes. I strongly support that aim, with reasonable allowances for individual ability and the help a person may need.

    A division of labour can make a household run smoothly. One person may enjoy cooking, another may handle laundry, and both can become efficient at their regular tasks. The difficulty is that a household organised entirely around fixed roles can become fragile. If the usual cook is away, a well-stocked kitchen is of limited use to someone who cannot prepare a simple meal. Basic competence provides a reserve: another person can step in without requiring detailed instructions for every movement. This matters during illness, a busy period at work or a change in living arrangements. It also gives people greater freedom to choose how to divide tasks, because the existing arrangement is no longer the only workable one.

    Learning the work can improve cooperation even when the division stays the same. Cleaning a bathroom once reveals small decisions that are easy to overlook from outside: which surfaces need attention, what supplies have run out and how long the task takes. That understanding can make requests for help more realistic and prevent one person's contribution from becoming invisible. The aim should include noticing what needs doing, as well as completing an assigned job. Otherwise, the person who usually manages the home may remain responsible for supervising everyone else's assistance.

    The expectation must still fit the people involved. Some adults cannot safely perform particular physical tasks, and others may need adapted equipment or clear support. Capability should be developed within those circumstances, without treating identical performance as the measure of fairness. For most shared households, teaching and practising a small range of essential tasks would make everyday life more resilient and the usual division of work easier to sustain.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0420

    Climate Change, Energy & Environmental Responsibility

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some residential districts are moving from separate heating systems in each building to a shared system serving the whole area.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    326 words

    Moving from individual heating systems to a shared district system changes more than the equipment behind a warm room. It changes how maintenance is organised, how decisions are made and how widely a failure may be felt. I see the development as positive where the collective system is designed around reliable service and accountable management.

    A shared arrangement can make specialist maintenance more practical. Instead of each building's occupants arranging their own repairs, a responsible operator can plan work across the system and maintain equipment intended for the combined demand. Changes to the main heat supply can also be organised for the district rather than negotiated separately for every building. Where the chosen source uses less energy or produces fewer emissions than the systems it replaces, the environmental benefit can reach many homes through one coordinated change. Sharing by itself does not establish that benefit; the actual source and performance still matter.

    Residents may also welcome having less equipment to manage individually. Yet the convenience brings dependence. A fault in a common part of the system can affect several buildings, and households may have limited ability to choose another supplier. Installation can involve disruptive work, while charges must cover both daily operation and future repairs. An attractive initial price is therefore an incomplete basis for judging the scheme. Residents need understandable bills, a clear route for complaints and credible arrangements for maintaining heat during repairs or interruptions.

    These concerns are reasons to design the shared service carefully. They do not remove the advantages of coordinated investment and maintenance, particularly where separate systems are already due for replacement. Before a district commits, the proposed costs, performance and responsibilities should be compared with the realistic alternatives. Residents should also have a meaningful say in decisions that will affect them for years. With those conditions in place, a common heating system can turn a collection of separate maintenance problems into a service that is easier to plan and sustain.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0422

    Wildlife, Habitats & Animal Protection

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some neighbouring landowners agree to manage parts of their land together to provide space for wildlife.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of this arrangement?

    Answer

    324 words

    A boundary that divides two properties need not divide the needs of the wildlife moving between them. When neighbouring landowners manage some land together, they can create a more coherent area for animals and plants. The arrangement can achieve more than isolated efforts, but its success depends on maintaining agreement among people with different priorities.

    The clearest advantage is coordination across the boundary. One owner might preserve a strip of vegetation leading towards a pond, while another protects the adjoining space. Taken together, those decisions can provide a route and a destination that neither plot would offer alone. Owners can also compare observations, share equipment and agree when particular work should take place. If one area needs attention, the cost and knowledge required need not rest with a single person. A joint plan makes it easier to see how each small contribution fits into a larger whole.

    The difficulties concern both land use and cooperation. Giving space to wildlife may reduce the area available for crops, grazing or other activities, and the sacrifice may be uneven. An owner contributing a particularly useful section of land might bear more cost than a neighbour who gains similar satisfaction from the project. Decisions about access, vegetation and maintenance can also produce disagreements. Even where everyone begins enthusiastically, illness, financial pressure or a change of ownership may leave part of the plan without support. The adjoining pieces still need to work together after the original conversation has ended.

    It is therefore sensible to begin with clear, achievable commitments and an agreed way to review them. Owners should understand what each person provides, how shared work is organised and what happens if someone needs to withdraw. Advice about the wildlife actually present can help ensure that well-meant changes are suitable for the site. Joint management offers a valuable way to connect land and effort, provided that the human arrangement is given as much practical attention as the physical one.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0441

    Natural Resources, Pollution & Disaster Preparation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some authorities offer to relocate households from areas repeatedly affected by flooding or other natural hazards rather than rebuild there each time.

    Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    330 words

    After repeated flooding, rebuilding a house may restore its rooms without restoring confidence in living there. Offering households a realistic route to a safer location can have greater benefits than rebuilding in the same place each time. I support this approach where the recurring danger is serious and the offer addresses the practical costs of moving.

    Relocation can interrupt a cycle of damage, temporary accommodation and repair. The gain is not confined to the building. Children may be able to attend school without repeated disruption, adults can plan work more reliably, and families can replace possessions without expecting to lose them again in the next event. Authorities may also avoid repeatedly funding emergency responses and reconstruction at the same sites. These advantages depend on the new location being properly assessed: moving a household into another vulnerable area would merely move the problem with it.

    The disadvantages are nevertheless considerable. A home is part of a network of work, neighbours, familiar services and personal memories. Replacing the structure does not automatically replace that network. A household offered a safer property far from employment may face a new and lasting financial difficulty. Others may lose nearby help with children or older relatives. Some residents will also attach great value to remaining in a place where their family has lived for years. These losses deserve direct attention, even when they cannot all be expressed as a sum of money.

    On balance, protection from serious repeated danger justifies offering relocation, but a useful offer needs more than a new address. Suitable housing, moving costs, access to essential services and reasonable links to employment should be considered together. Households need clear information and time to compare the options, including whether protection at the existing site is feasible. Because the policy is an offer, it can create a choice for people who currently lack one. Its greatest advantage is the possibility of rebuilding an ordinary, dependable daily life in a place where that life can continue.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0471

    Public Transport, Roads & Commuting

    問題へ戻る ↗

    People sometimes avoid public transport because connections between different services are unreliable.

    Why do these connection problems arise? What could improve the experience of passengers who need to change services?

    Answer

    325 words

    A passenger can spend a bus journey watching the minutes until a connecting train, only to arrive as its doors close. When such connections are unreliable, the uncertainty affects the whole trip. Problems commonly arise because services are planned separately and delays are handled without enough regard for passengers travelling between them.

    A timetable may suit each operator while leaving too little time for an actual transfer. Walking between stops, finding a platform or moving with luggage takes time that a line on a schedule does not reveal. Different ticketing arrangements can add another queue. Meanwhile, traffic or a late departure can disturb even a reasonable connection. If each operator concentrates on keeping its own next service punctual, nobody may be responsible for the journey that requires both services.

    Improvement should therefore begin with coordinated planning. Operators can examine common transfer points, allow realistic walking time and align services where many passengers need to change. Clear signs, accessible routes and simpler ticketing remove avoidable delays within the interchange. These changes address the ordinary journey rather than relying entirely on staff to rescue a connection after it has already become doubtful.

    Some disruption will remain, so passengers also need a workable response when plans fail. Accurate information should explain whether the connection is likely to be made and what alternative is available. Operators could agree limited waiting arrangements where holding one service briefly prevents a much longer delay for transferring passengers. Such decisions must consider people already aboard, since rescuing one connection can otherwise cause another to be missed. Where waiting is impractical, a clear onward option is more useful than a display that merely confirms the delay.

    The aim is a journey whose separate stages fit together reliably enough for passengers to plan around them. Better timetables, usable interchanges and shared responsibility for disruption can all contribute. Information helps people cope, but the strongest improvement is to give them fewer failed connections to cope with.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0492

    Tourism, Travel & Local Communities

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people believe customs presented to tourists should remain as close as possible to their traditional form. Others think adapting them to visitors' expectations is reasonable.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    337 words

    Presenting a custom to visitors involves choices about what they will see, hear and understand. Keeping close to its traditional form can protect its meaning, while some adaptation can make it accessible to an unfamiliar audience. I favour limited, openly explained changes chosen by the people who practise the custom, with its central purpose kept in view.

    Those who argue for preservation are concerned that a custom may lose the very qualities that make it worth encountering. A seasonal ceremony, for example, may have a particular place in the life of a community. Performing selected parts every evening for a short tourist programme could remove their relationship with that season and with one another. Visitors might leave believing they had seen the whole custom when they had seen only an entertaining extract. Retaining the original sequence, setting and purpose allows people to encounter something that asks for their attention on its own terms.

    Adaptation can nevertheless help visitors understand and support a tradition. Translation, a brief explanation or a demonstration at an accessible time can make participation possible for someone with limited knowledge. Performers may reasonably adjust the length of a public presentation so that it can fit alongside their other work. Income from visitors could help pay for materials, practice and teaching, allowing skills to continue. A custom also belongs to living practitioners, who may wish to change it for their own reasons; an outsider's expectation of complete historical stillness should not decide their choices.

    The important distinction is between helping an audience approach a custom and quietly replacing its meaning with whatever is easiest to sell. Communities should decide which elements can be shared, adapted or kept private. A shortened demonstration should be described as such, with enough context to explain what has been omitted. On that basis, adaptation can be reasonable without making tourists' expectations the sole measure of value. Visitors gain a clearer understanding when the presentation is honest about both what they are seeing and the larger life to which it belongs.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0513

    Aviation, Long-distance Travel & International Mobility

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Transport companies should provide practical assistance to passengers whose long-distance journeys are seriously disrupted, regardless of who caused the disruption.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    333 words

    When a long-distance journey breaks down, passengers still need to know where to go and how to get there. Those needs arise before responsibility for the disruption has necessarily been established. I strongly agree that transport companies should provide practical assistance regardless of the cause, while the form and cost of that help should remain proportionate.

    The main reason is that the company is usually better placed than an individual passenger to organise the next step. It can explain the status of its services, identify onward options and coordinate with staff at other locations. A traveller stranded far from home may lack local knowledge, a reliable connection or somewhere suitable to wait. Clear guidance, help with rebooking and access to basic facilities can prevent uncertainty from turning into a more serious problem. These actions remain useful whether the original cause was a company failure, severe weather or an incident elsewhere on the route.
