    Providing assistance should also be distinguished from accepting blame. A company can help a passenger find accommodation without agreeing that it caused the need for an overnight stay. Questions about compensation or reimbursement can be considered separately. Even when a traveller has contributed to the difficulty, staff can still explain available options and help them make a safe, workable plan. Refusing all help until every cause is settled would leave the immediate problem waiting for an investigation.

    There are practical limits. A major disruption may affect many passengers at once, while rooms, seats and staff time remain scarce. Companies need a clear order of priorities, including attention to people who face particular difficulties, and honest information when a solution cannot be provided immediately. The costs of assistance also need to be planned for rather than left to improvised decisions at a crowded desk. My agreement concerns a dependable responsibility to help passengers through the disruption, with financial liability considered on its own grounds. The first response should make the next few hours more manageable; the account of responsibility can follow.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0531

    School Education & the Curriculum

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some schools are introducing dedicated lessons in which pupils consider ethical questions arising in everyday life.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    327 words

    A pupil who finds a friend's private message on a shared screen faces a question that knowing how to use the device does not answer. Should they read it, ignore it or tell someone? Dedicated lessons on everyday ethical questions can give pupils time to examine such choices. I regard their introduction as a positive development when discussion is thoughtful and connected to ordinary conduct.

    One benefit is learning to explain a judgement. Pupils can distinguish what happened, what they assume and whose interests are affected before deciding what should be done. In the example of the message, curiosity, privacy and concern for a friend may pull in different directions. A further detail could change the decision: a message suggesting immediate danger raises a different concern from a harmless private conversation. Working through those differences teaches pupils to revise a judgement for a reason, rather than simply repeat the first confident answer offered in the room.

    Lessons can also make disagreement more manageable. Pupils may discover that another person values something they had overlooked, or that two apparently opposed answers rely on different assumptions. A teacher can help them ask questions, give reasons and listen without turning a disagreement into a judgement of the other person's character. These habits are relevant to group work, friendships and the shared rules of school life. The value lies in practising the discussion as well as reaching a conclusion.

    There are risks if the subject becomes a test of guessing the teacher's preferred view. Assessment should reward careful reasoning and respectful engagement, with clear boundaries where conduct could harm others. Pupils should be able to discuss fictional cases without being pressed to disclose private experiences. Nor can a weekly lesson compensate for unfair behaviour elsewhere in the school. With those safeguards, dedicated time offers a useful opportunity to connect principles with decisions that pupils recognise. Its success should be visible in how they consider and explain those decisions beyond the classroom.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0537

    School Education & the Curriculum

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Learning how to assess the reliability of information should be a compulsory part of school education.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    330 words

    School pupils encounter information long before they are asked to write a formal research project. A message from a friend, a convincing photograph and a confident explanation can each appear to deserve belief. I strongly agree that learning to assess reliability should be compulsory, provided that it becomes a practical habit across subjects rather than a list of warning signs learnt for a test.

    The first benefit is a clearer understanding of what a claim rests on. Pupils can learn to ask who produced a statement, what evidence supports it and whether that evidence actually answers the question being asked. For example, a photograph may establish that a crowd was present without showing how most people in a country felt. The picture has not become useless; the conclusion has simply grown larger than the picture can support. Recognising that difference is useful in history, science and everyday discussion.

    Compulsory teaching also gives every pupil access to methods that might otherwise depend on help at home. Lessons should include comparing accounts, tracing a quotation to its context and distinguishing a direct observation from an interpretation. Teachers can demonstrate how a reasonable judgement changes when new information arrives. Changing an answer for a stated reason should be presented as part of careful thinking, rather than as an embarrassment to hide.

    There are risks if this teaching becomes a general lesson in suspicion. A polished source can be wrong, but an unfamiliar source is not wrong merely because it is unfamiliar. Equally, finding two disagreeing claims does not make them equally well supported. Pupils need guided practice with evidence, appropriate subject knowledge and an honest recognition of what they cannot yet judge. No short checklist can remove those demands.

    I would therefore include information assessment throughout compulsory education, with tasks suited to pupils' age and knowledge. The aim should be neither automatic belief nor automatic rejection. It should be the ability to give a proportionate reason for accepting, doubting or postponing a conclusion.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0551

    Higher Education, Fees & Student Life

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some universities require first-year students to take common introductory courses before they choose a particular degree subject.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of this approach?

    Answer

    340 words

    A degree subject can look quite different in a prospectus and in a room where someone is actually teaching it. Requiring new university students to take common introductory courses gives them a chance to discover that difference before committing themselves. The approach offers better-informed choices and a shared foundation, although it can also delay useful specialist work.

    Its clearest advantage concerns students whose preferences are still taking shape. Someone attracted to psychology might enjoy its questions about people but find its statistical work unexpectedly demanding. An introductory course allows this discovery to happen while changing direction is relatively straightforward. Exposure to neighbouring subjects can also reveal connections that a narrow course would leave unexplored. A future engineer who has studied environmental questions may be better prepared to consider what a design will do beyond the drawing board.

    A common programme can additionally give students a shared starting point. They arrive from schools with different resources and may have very different experience of academic writing or evaluating evidence. Teaching these skills together makes later expectations clearer. It also allows students to meet people outside their eventual department, widening both their friendships and the range of ideas they encounter.

    However, the same common courses may feel wasteful to someone who already knows their subject well. Time spent repeating familiar material is time unavailable for advanced study. If these requirements extend the degree, they can also add substantially to students’ living costs. Breadth can become thinness if a programme offers a succession of brief introductions without enough time to understand any of them. Students would then postpone their choice without becoming much better equipped to make it.

    The value of this arrangement therefore depends on its design and the students entering it. A well-connected programme, with routes past material already mastered, can make exploration productive. A rigid programme risks treating every beginner as if they were beginning in exactly the same place. Common courses are most useful when they provide a dependable foundation while leaving room for genuine differences in preparation and purpose.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0569

    Language Learning, Literacy & Communication

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people believe beginners should first learn a large stock of useful words and expressions. Others believe they should first develop a clear understanding of sentence structure.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    333 words

    Beginners need something useful to say, but they also need a way to say something they have not already learnt. This explains the attraction of both a substantial stock of expressions and a clear account of sentence structure. I would begin with a manageable set of useful words and phrases, and introduce the relevant structures through their use, rather than postpone either part until the other is complete.

    The case for learning expressions first is practical. A learner who can ask for help, explain a simple preference or recognise an everyday request can participate immediately. Familiar phrases also provide examples of how words fit together. A person may learn 'I'm looking for' as a useful unit before being able to describe its grammar. That early success can give further study a purpose: the next expression is connected to something the learner wants to do.

    However, accumulating a large stock without examining relationships can leave the beginner dependent on remembered situations. A sentence that worked yesterday may not express today's time, intention or degree of certainty. Understanding structure helps the learner alter an example responsibly. Changing the subject, making a question or adding a condition becomes a controlled operation instead of a guess based on the sound of a familiar phrase.

    The opposing approach has its own limit. A clear grammatical explanation supplies little to communicate if the learner has no usable vocabulary or experience of the form in context. I would therefore teach a small group of expressions around an actual purpose, draw attention to a useful pattern, and ask the learner to adapt it. For instance, asking about an opening time can lead naturally to asking about a different place or a different day. The meaning changes in a visible way, and the form changes with it.

    Neither a large phrase collection nor an abstract structural map should have to be finished before communication begins. Useful language gives beginners a starting point; an increasing understanding of structure lets them move beyond it.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0574

    Language Learning, Literacy & Communication

    問題へ戻る ↗

    People who use more than one language sometimes feel that each language connects them to a different part of their identity.

    How can language create a sense of belonging? How important is it to maintain these different connections?

    Answer

    324 words

    A language can connect a person to a group through much more than the information it carries. It may hold the familiar rhythm of family conversation, the terms of a shared activity or the small jokes that need no explanation. These connections can support different parts of an identity. I consider maintaining them valuable, although their importance and form will vary between individuals.

    Belonging often develops through repeated participation. Using a language with relatives allows someone to share memories and take part in ordinary exchanges, including disagreements. In another language, the same person may take part in professional discussions or friendships formed later in life. Neither relationship has to be less authentic. Different surroundings call attention to different knowledge and habits, so a speaker may experience a change of emphasis without becoming a different person altogether.

    Language can also give access to particular ways of expressing affection, humour or respect. A phrase may be understood by outsiders in a literal sense while carrying a longer history for those who use it together. Maintaining the language preserves opportunities to participate in that history. Books, conversations and community activities can keep the connection active even when daily life takes place elsewhere.

    Nevertheless, maintaining every connection equally may be neither possible nor desirable. People's circumstances change, and their relationship with a community may include difficulty as well as warmth. Someone should not be judged disloyal merely because one language becomes less fluent or less central to their life. Nor should a language be treated as a boundary that prevents new members from belonging. The aim is to preserve meaningful choices, including the choice to reshape an inherited connection.

    I would therefore encourage opportunities to use different languages without imposing a fixed account of what each must mean to its speaker. The value lies in continued access to people, memories and ways of understanding. A person's linguistic connections can remain distinct while still belonging to one developing life.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0577

    Language Learning, Literacy & Communication

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some travellers rely on translation devices instead of learning any of the local language.

    Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    340 words

    A translation device can make a journey possible for someone who would otherwise struggle to ask for a ticket or explain where they need to go. Its advantages are substantial. Even so, I do not think they outweigh the disadvantages when using the device becomes a reason to learn none of the local language. That is a much stronger choice than taking a useful tool along.

    The immediate benefit is access. A traveller cannot reasonably learn every language they may encounter, especially on a short visit involving several countries. A device can help them read unfamiliar signs, understand a menu and communicate requests that exceed their limited vocabulary. It also offers a measure of independence: they need not find an English speaker every time an ordinary difficulty arises. For a brief stop, this may be the only practical way to manage more complicated exchanges.

    Complete reliance, however, leaves the traveller dependent on the device being available and its output being understood. A flat battery can turn a manageable question into a considerable obstacle. Less visibly, a translation may sound plausible while missing the intended sense, and someone who knows nothing of the language has fewer ways to notice. Passing a screen across a counter does not always reveal whether the person reading it has understood the request or merely recognised the words.

    There is also a modest but valuable part of travel that a device cannot undertake on its owner's behalf. Saying a greeting, thanking a host or asking permission creates direct contact. These exchanges require little study compared with fluency, yet they let the traveller participate in the encounter rather than organise every turn through a screen. They offer useful practice in listening and responding as well.

    The fairest comparison is therefore between total dependence and using the same device alongside a few practical expressions. The latter retains nearly all the technological benefits while reducing avoidable difficulties. Translation tools deserve a place in a traveller's pocket; a little knowledge of the language deserves a place in the journey too.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0586

    Learning Methods, Teachers & Educational Opportunity

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some students treat mistakes as useful information, while others see them as evidence that they lack ability.

    What shapes these reactions? How can they influence future learning?

    Answer

    329 words

    Two students can make the same mistake and take away very different messages. One sees a particular point that needs work; the other sees a verdict on their ability. These reactions are shaped by previous experience, the responses of other people and the student's understanding of learning. They can influence both whether practice continues and what that practice achieves.

    Feedback is an important source of interpretation. If a teacher identifies an error clearly and shows how to investigate it, the student has something definite to do next. A comment such as 'This step assumes the two quantities are equal' directs attention to a relationship that can be checked. A broad judgement about being careless or untalented gives less useful information and can make the whole person seem to be the problem. Family expectations and repeated comparisons with classmates may strengthen either response.

    Earlier experiences also matter. A student who has improved after struggling has a reason to regard an initial failure as temporary. Someone who has repeatedly worked hard without understanding why an answer is wrong may find that interpretation less convincing. The difficulty of the task, available support and the importance of the assessment can all affect the meaning attached to an error. Reaction is therefore not simply a permanent feature of character.

    The consequences appear in later choices. Treating mistakes as information can encourage students to inspect their methods, ask precise questions and try again with a change. Treating them as proof of incapacity may lead to avoidance or to choosing only tasks that already feel safe. Yet merely calling every mistake useful is insufficient: repeating an unsuccessful method without diagnosis is still repetition. An error becomes a resource when it changes the learner's understanding or next action.

    These reactions can consequently widen or narrow future learning opportunities. Students benefit from a realistic distinction between a current gap in knowledge and a final limit on ability, supported by feedback that makes improvement something they can actually attempt.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0590

    Learning Methods, Teachers & Educational Opportunity

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some students remain silent when they do not understand a lesson instead of asking the teacher for help.

    Why does this happen? What could make it easier for students to ask questions?

    Answer

    355 words

    When a teacher asks whether everyone understands and hears nothing, the silence can be comforting. It is also difficult to interpret. Students may remain quiet because asking feels socially risky, because they cannot yet identify their difficulty, or because the lesson leaves little room for a question. Making questions easier requires attention to all three possibilities.

    The social risk is sometimes the most immediate. A student may fear appearing less capable than classmates, particularly if previous questions have attracted laughter or an impatient reply. Even a friendly teacher can unintentionally discourage questions by praising speed so consistently that hesitation begins to look like failure. In such a classroom, a student can preserve the appearance of understanding by saying nothing, although the difficulty itself remains.

    Other students would gladly ask if they knew what to ask. When several unfamiliar ideas arrive together, they may not be able to locate the first point at which the explanation stopped making sense. A broad invitation to raise a question then demands precisely the clarity they lack. Some also need time to organise their thoughts, especially when studying in a language they are still learning. The teacher may have moved on before the question is ready.

    Teachers can respond by making uncertainty both acceptable and easier to describe. They can pause after an important step, allow a brief discussion in pairs and ask students to identify which part needs another example. A choice between two possible explanations may reveal a misunderstanding more readily than asking whether everything is clear. Written questions or a short conversation after class offer another route for students who are reluctant to speak publicly. These routes should complement, rather than replace, opportunities to ask during the lesson.

    The teacher's response then determines whether the invitation will be trusted next time. A question needs a patient answer, or an honest promise to return to it, without treating its author as an inconvenience. Over time, asking for clarification can become an ordinary part of learning. The aim is not simply a noisier classroom, but one in which silence is no longer the easiest way to hide a difficulty.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0619

    Employment, Career Choices & Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people believe workers should develop deep expertise in one field. Others believe having a wide range of skills provides better career opportunities.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    340 words

    The most useful worker is not always the one who can list the greatest number of skills. Much depends on how well those skills answer a real need. Deep expertise can make a person dependable in demanding work, while a broader range can open routes into different roles. In my view, depth should usually provide the foundation of a career, with wider skills connecting that foundation to new opportunities.

    The argument for specialisation is strongest where mistakes are difficult to detect or expensive to repair. An experienced furniture maker, for example, can choose a joint that will remain sound after years of use. The customer may see a neat surface; the maker must understand what is happening beneath it. Such judgement takes sustained practice. Employers and clients have reason to value someone who can handle unusual problems as well as familiar ones, and this can support a lasting professional reputation.

    Breadth, however, affects where that expertise can be used. The same maker may need to estimate costs, discuss a design with customers and organise deliveries. These abilities do not replace craftsmanship, but they can turn it into a viable business. In a larger organisation, workers who understand neighbouring roles may also explain problems more clearly and help colleagues work together. They have more ways to contribute when the shape of a project changes.

    There are circumstances in which exploring widely deserves priority. Someone entering employment may need experience of several kinds of work before finding a suitable field. A worker whose industry is contracting may likewise need to move beyond an established speciality. Yet breadth without sufficient competence in any area can leave a person able to describe many tasks and unable to carry one through independently.

    I would therefore favour a career built around something a person can do reliably, while continuing to acquire skills that extend its use. The balance can change over time. What matters is that learning produces both substantial capability and room to move, rather than an impressive list with little dependable work behind it.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0626

    Workplace Practices & Work-life Balance

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Employers should give staff reasonable notice of changes to their work schedules, even when this reduces business flexibility.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    342 words

    A work schedule organises far more than the hours spent at work. Around it, employees arrange childcare, transport, study and time with other people. I strongly agree that employers should give reasonable notice of changes, even when this limits business flexibility. Predictability is part of a workable employment relationship, and its value should be included in business decisions.

    The strongest reason is the uneven burden of a last-minute change. A manager may move a shift on a screen in a few seconds. The employee then has to contact a childminder, cancel an appointment, find another bus or ask someone else to rearrange their day. Each change travels further than the workplace. If the new shift is compulsory, the employee may have little choice about accepting these costs, although these costs may not appear in the employer's calculation of flexibility.

    Advance notice allows these arrangements to be made with less disruption. It can also make work more dependable for the employer: staff who know when they are needed have a better chance of arriving rested and prepared. This does not mean that every business can promise identical hours indefinitely. A restaurant may face uncertain bookings, and a small team may need to cover unexpected absence. These difficulties are real, but they support careful contingency planning rather than routine surprise for employees.

    Reasonable notice should therefore reflect the type of work and the scale of the proposed change. Employers can publish schedules early, maintain a voluntary system for extra shifts and explain clearly when exceptional changes may be necessary. Staff should have a practical opportunity to decline changes that conflict with important commitments. Where urgent cover is essential, additional payment or time off can acknowledge the disruption, although compensation cannot always restore a missed event.

    I would allow genuine emergencies to justify shorter notice, with an explanation and fair treatment afterwards. The normal expectation should remain stable schedules and timely communication. A business needs room to respond to demand, but it should plan on the basis that its employees also have commitments worth keeping.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0659

    Personal Finance, Saving & Financial Education

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some financial services automatically move small amounts of a customer's money into savings as part of their everyday account use.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    333 words

    Automatic transfers of small sums into savings can be a positive development, provided customers choose the arrangement and can readily control it. The service makes a useful intention easier to carry out. Its success, however, depends on whether the money being moved is genuinely available to save.

    For someone with a little money left over each month, the main benefit is regularity. Saving often requires a decision that can be postponed while more immediate purchases occupy attention. An automatic transfer removes that repeated decision. A few small sums can accumulate quietly until there is enough to meet a modest unexpected expense. The customer may find that a balance which once existed only as a good intention has become something they can actually use.

    The same process can cause trouble when an account has little spare money. Consider a customer whose income arrives irregularly and whose rent is due before the next payment. Several individually small transfers may leave too little in the everyday account at the wrong moment. The total amount owned has not increased; it has simply changed location. If retrieving it is awkward, or if the service charges fees, apparent convenience can create an additional burden.

    Good design should make this distinction clear. Customers need to see how much will move, choose a limit and pause transfers without difficulty. A service could stop moving money when the available balance falls below a level selected by the customer. Any charges should be easy to understand, and saved funds intended for everyday emergencies should remain accessible. These controls matter more than a cheerful display announcing that another small sum has been saved.

    Overall, I favour this development as a convenient aid for people whose circumstances suit it. It can support a habit without demanding attention every day, but it cannot supply income that is missing or make essential spending disappear. The most helpful service would leave customers with both a growing reserve and a clear view of the money they still need now.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0662

    Business, Trade & Corporate Responsibility

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some businesses guarantee that the prices paid by their regular customers will remain unchanged for a full year.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of offering this guarantee?

    Answer

    331 words

    A promise that prices will remain unchanged for a year gives regular customers something concrete on which to plan. It can strengthen their relationship with a business, but it also commits that business to carrying risks which would otherwise be shared through price changes. The advantages are greatest when both the firm's costs and its customers' needs are reasonably predictable.

    For customers, the principal benefit is certainty. A small firm buying the same materials each month can prepare a budget without wondering what each delivery will cost. A household paying regularly for a service gains similar reassurance. The supplier may benefit in turn because a clear promise gives customers a reason to keep returning. Stable demand can make staffing, purchasing and delivery schedules easier to organise. There is also a practical simplicity to the arrangement: less time is spent checking new prices or explaining increases, leaving both sides free to attend to the service itself.

    The difficulty is that a fixed selling price does not fix every cost behind it. Materials, transport or rent may become more expensive during the year, while the promised price remains exactly where it was. The business must absorb the difference. A firm with narrow margins could find itself delivering more orders without earning enough to sustain them. It might set a higher price at the beginning to allow for uncertainty, reducing the guarantee's appeal. Customers also face a possible disadvantage if competing prices fall: an unchanged price is predictable, but it is not necessarily the best available price. The guarantee alone gives no reason to assume they are prevented from shopping elsewhere.

    Offering such a guarantee therefore trades some flexibility for a more dependable relationship. It can work well for repeat purchases whose costs are manageable, especially when customers value budgeting and continuity. Businesses need to calculate whether they can honour the promise throughout the year, while customers should compare its price as well as its duration before deciding how much the certainty is worth.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0684

    Crime, Justice & Rehabilitation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    For some offences, victims and offenders are offered the opportunity to meet with a trained mediator, provided that both sides agree.

    Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    337 words

    For suitable offences, a voluntary meeting between a victim and an offender can provide something that a formal decision alone may leave unresolved. It gives the people directly affected a structured opportunity to ask questions, describe harm and consider responsibility. With a trained mediator and continuing consent, I believe these advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages, although the meeting should remain an additional option rather than an expected duty.

    The main benefit is the chance to make the consequences of an offence specific. A damaged shop window may be recorded as a financial loss. The shopkeeper might also want to explain the hours spent clearing glass, the interrupted work and the uncertainty about whether it will happen again. Hearing this can help an offender understand the extent of the harm. The victim, meanwhile, may be able to ask questions that matter personally, such as why that shop was chosen. A carefully managed conversation can also support practical agreements about repairing damage. Its value lies partly in giving the victim some choice over what is discussed.

    Nevertheless, willingness to attend does not guarantee that the encounter will be helpful. An offender may minimise the harm or give an apology that the victim finds unconvincing. The victim may leave more distressed, even though both parties initially agreed to meet. A trained mediator can prepare participants and intervene, but cannot promise a particular emotional outcome. There is also a risk that others will treat reconciliation as the desirable result and place subtle pressure on the victim to forgive. Participation and forgiveness must remain separate choices. Any agreement should be realistic, and the process should allow either person to stop if the meeting becomes harmful.

    On balance, these risks justify careful preparation and clear limits rather than abandoning the opportunity. The potential gains are substantial because participants can address personal questions and practical consequences that might otherwise receive little attention. Success should be judged by whether the meeting serves their needs and supports responsibility, without requiring a shared feeling at its end.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0718

    Government, Democracy & Public Participation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some residents find it difficult to complete routine tasks such as applying for permits or registering for public services.

    Why can these tasks be difficult? What can governments do to make the process easier?

    Answer

    342 words

    Routine public administration can become difficult when a process is designed around the government's departments rather than the resident's task. Applying for one permit may involve several forms, unfamiliar terms and documents whose purpose is never explained. Differences in language, confidence and access to technology add further obstacles. Governments can reduce these difficulties by designing complete, understandable routes through each service and providing help where it is needed.

    One cause is fragmentation. A resident may supply information to one office only to be asked for it again by another, in a slightly different form. Each office may regard its own request as simple, while nobody considers the whole sequence. Instructions can also assume knowledge that applicants do not possess. If a form asks for a reference number without saying where to find it, the resident must interrupt the application to solve a new problem. Repeating this experience makes even a short form exhausting.

    Digital services can add their own demands. Someone may have internet access but struggle to upload a document, remember several passwords or understand an error message. Others need a large-print version, language support or an opportunity to explain an unusual situation to a person. Governments should therefore test procedures with residents who have different needs. Instructions should identify the documents required before the application begins, explain unfamiliar terms and show what will happen next. Where lawful and appropriate, departments could reuse information already supplied, with clear safeguards and an opportunity to correct it.

    Assistance also needs to be easy to reach. A telephone line or local service desk should help people complete the task, including resolving difficulties that fall between departments. Online forms can save progress and identify the exact missing item instead of rejecting an entire application. Clear time estimates and status updates would reduce unnecessary enquiries. The aim should be a process that an unfamiliar applicant can follow from beginning to end, with support for exceptions. Measuring that complete experience would give governments a better guide to improvement than counting how many forms they have put online.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0729

    Inequality, Migration & Social Responsibility

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that newcomers should receive separate support services while they settle in a country. Others believe that they should use the same services as long-term residents from the beginning.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    341 words

    Newcomers need public services they can actually use while learning how life in a new country works. Separate support can address unfamiliar procedures and immediate difficulties, whereas shared services can encourage equal treatment and everyday contact. I favour access to ordinary services from the outset, supported by specialist help where a person's circumstances require it.

    The case for separate provision begins with the concentration of unfamiliar tasks after arrival. Someone may need to register for healthcare, find a school and understand a tenancy agreement within the same few weeks. A dedicated service can explain how these tasks fit together, provide language assistance and direct people to suitable advice. Staff who regularly work with new arrivals may recognise difficulties that a general service overlooks. Instead of sending someone from office to office, they can help establish a manageable sequence. For people with limited local knowledge or particular support needs, this can make the initial period less confusing.

    However, using the same services as established residents also has important advantages. It makes equal access visible and gives newcomers experience of the systems they will continue to use. Shared schools, community centres and advice services can create ordinary opportunities to meet people beyond a recently arrived group. Separate provision may duplicate resources and require an awkward transition later. There is also no reason to assume that every newcomer needs the same help: a fluent speaker with family nearby may have fewer difficulties than a long-term resident facing a sudden personal crisis.

    The practical solution is therefore a common system with additional assistance that people can enter and leave according to need. Specialist staff could work alongside general services, help with the first applications and remain available for complex questions. A separate introductory programme can be useful without becoming a separate route through everyday life. Funding should follow the actual support required, and progress should be judged by whether people can obtain services confidently and independently. This approach preserves the expertise of dedicated support while giving newcomers a place in shared institutions from the beginning.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0749

    Arts, Heritage & Public Funding

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Organisations receiving public funding for the arts should provide opportunities for people to take part, as well as opportunities to watch professional performances.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    341 words

    Publicly funded arts organisations should generally give people opportunities to make and practise art as well as enjoy professional work. I agree with this requirement, provided the opportunities suit the organisation and do not undermine its central artistic activity. Public support can reasonably carry an expectation of participation, but participation needs to be meaningful.

    Professional performances depend on substantial preparation. Musicians need rehearsal time, and a theatre must bring writing, acting, design and technical work together. Public funding helps sustain this expertise and can keep the resulting performances affordable. Adding public activities creates a further responsibility: skilled performers may need support to teach beginners, and workshops require suitable space and preparation. If participation is imposed without resources, an organisation could struggle to do either job well. The requirement should build on its artistic strengths rather than simply add another item to its schedule.

    There is nevertheless a strong case for opening some of the creative process to the public. A local theatre might run a short course in writing dialogue, invite residents to develop a scene together and arrange for actors to help them revise it. Participants would encounter choices about language, pace and character that are less visible from a seat in the auditorium. They could also discover an interest they had never had a chance to pursue. Suitable activities need not produce polished work. Their value can lie in sustained attention, shared effort and the experience of making something that did not exist before.

    Such provision requires time, teaching skills and accessible arrangements. A small company may be able to offer a well-run workshop each season, while a large institution can support a continuing programme. Funding bodies should recognise these differences and cover the additional work, rather than reward the largest attendance figures regardless of quality. Overall, I support participation as a normal part of publicly funded arts provision, alongside excellent professional performances. The appropriate requirement is a real, supported chance to take part, designed around the organisation's expertise and matched by enough resources to make the experience worthwhile.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0780

    News, Journalism & Public Information

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some news organisations now publish clear explanations whenever they correct a significant error, including what went wrong in the reporting process.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    323 words

    Publishing clear explanations of significant reporting errors is a positive development. Readers need to know both what the correct information is and why the earlier account went wrong. An explanation cannot remove the original harm, but it can help people repair their understanding and judge the reliability of future reporting more accurately.

    Consider a report announcing that a local library will close when closure is still only a proposal. Readers might change their plans or criticise a decision that has not been taken. A quiet replacement of the article would leave those who saw the first version uncertain about what to believe. A visible correction can identify the mistaken statement, set out the actual position and explain whether the error arose from a misunderstood document or a failure to check with the relevant organisation. The sequence matters: readers first need the right information, then enough context to understand the mistake.

    Explaining the process also creates a basis for accountability. If an organisation says that an important claim was published without a necessary check, it can describe how that check will be handled in future. Readers then have something more useful than a general assurance that standards are high. This openness may initially reduce confidence by revealing weaknesses, but confidence based on an accurate view of those weaknesses is preferable to confidence maintained by concealment. Repeated errors would still require serious scrutiny; repeated explanations alone would not demonstrate improvement.

    There are limits to what should be published. An account of the process need not expose a confidential source or speculate about an individual reporter's motives. It should be proportionate, readable and easy to find, with the correction stated clearly enough to avoid spreading the false claim again. Within these limits, explaining significant errors is a responsible part of journalism. It helps the public distinguish the corrected facts from the earlier interpretation and gives the organisation a concrete obligation to improve the way it works.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0784

    Entertainment, Celebrity & Cultural Life

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some entertainment venues organise events designed for adults and children to enjoy together, rather than providing separate activities for different age groups.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of this approach?

    Answer

    336 words

    Events intended for adults and children together can turn entertainment into a shared occasion. They give families and mixed-age groups something to experience in common, with fewer arrangements to make. Their main difficulty is finding a programme that allows different people to enjoy themselves without continually asking one group to accommodate the other.

    One advantage is the conversation that can continue after the event. Adults and children have seen the same performance, but may have noticed quite different things. A comic play, for example, can offer visible action that younger children enjoy while also rewarding adults' attention to the language. Afterwards, each can add something to the other's account. Shared events can also be easier to organise. Adults need not arrange supervision elsewhere while attending their own activity, and children can take part with someone familiar nearby. For a venue, attracting the whole group may help build a relationship with families who return as their children grow.

    However, a common programme must choose a time, a pace and a level of noise. A late performance may suit adults but leave a small child tired before the most interesting scene arrives. Repeated explanations for younger visitors can interrupt the experience for older ones, while material aimed mainly at adults may leave children with little to follow. The problem is not that either group has the wrong preferences. The event is trying to satisfy several sets of needs within the same limited space and time. If it succeeds only by removing everything challenging, the result may interest nobody for long.

    This approach consequently works best when organisers design for several levels of engagement and explain clearly which ages an event is likely to suit. Short breaks, accessible facilities and opportunities for optional participation can help, although they cannot make every event suitable for every family. Joint activities offer valuable shared experiences, but venues should retain some age-specific choices as well. A varied programme allows people to enjoy time together without making togetherness the condition of every enjoyable outing.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0819

    Digital Communication, Social Media & Privacy

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some families use digital services that allow relatives to see one another’s location throughout the day.

    Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    341 words

    Seeing where a relative is can make everyday arrangements easier and provide reassurance when someone is travelling. However, sharing locations throughout the day gives a family far more information than most particular arrangements require. I believe the disadvantages generally outweigh the advantages as a routine practice, although limited sharing can be useful in agreed circumstances.

    The practical benefits are clear. If a parent is collecting a teenager from a station, location sharing can show whether they have arrived and reduce repeated messages. A relative on an unfamiliar journey may also welcome someone knowing their progress. In a family where everyone freely chooses the arrangement, it can feel like a small convenience rather than an intrusion. These benefits deserve recognition, especially when the alternative is a series of anxious calls that the traveller cannot conveniently answer.

    The difficulty begins when an available location becomes an expected explanation. A person stops somewhere on the way home; a relative notices; a question follows. Nothing harmful need have happened, yet an ordinary detour now requires an account. Over time, continuous access can create pressure to remain visible, even after the original agreement no longer feels comfortable. It may also encourage mistaken conclusions. A point on a map does not explain why someone is there, who they are with or whether they need help. Family members can feel informed while still misunderstanding the situation.

    These costs concern independence and trust, whereas many of the benefits can be obtained through narrower arrangements. Sharing for a particular journey, agreeing an arrival message or enabling access only when help is requested can preserve useful reassurance. For young children or relatives with particular care needs, a different balance may be justified, with their wishes considered as far as possible. Even then, access should be proportionate and regularly discussed. I would therefore reserve location sharing for clear purposes instead of treating permanent visibility as an ordinary family obligation. The ability to check a location should remain a choice people can revisit, without having to defend their wish for some private time.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0824

    Artificial Intelligence, Automation & Human Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that artificial intelligence research should aim to reproduce human ways of thinking. Others believe that it should focus on solving practical tasks, regardless of how humans perform them.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    327 words

    Artificial intelligence research can ask how human thinking works, or how a machine might perform a useful task. The two questions sometimes meet, but answering one does not automatically answer the other. I believe both deserve investigation, with the aim of each project stated clearly rather than human imitation becoming a universal measure of success.

    Research inspired by human cognition can be valuable because it makes theories more precise. A proposal about how people remember or learn becomes easier to examine when its assumptions must be expressed in a working model. Researchers can compare the model's behaviour with human performance and investigate where the two diverge. However, producing a similar answer does not establish that the same process produced it. A convincing imitation may be a useful observation while leaving the underlying explanation unsettled.

    For many practical tasks, reproducing human methods is unnecessary. A system designed to organise delivery routes should be judged partly by whether its plans are workable, efficient and responsive to changing conditions. It need not follow the mental steps of an experienced driver to be useful. Requiring human resemblance in every such project could exclude approaches that exploit the different strengths of computation. Human habits themselves should not be treated as a guarantee of accuracy.

    Nevertheless, practical success needs a broader definition than achieving a high result on a narrow test. Researchers should examine failure, the conditions in which a system can be relied on and the consequences for its users. Human understanding can matter here without becoming a requirement that the machine think as a person does. A useful explanation for a user and a theory of human cognition are related concerns, but they remain different research products.

    I would therefore support a portfolio of approaches. Some projects should use computational models to investigate human thought; others should seek dependable solutions by different routes. Their value is clearest when the claim made for a result matches the question the research actually addressed.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0828

    Artificial Intelligence, Automation & Human Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that students should use artificial intelligence tools from the beginning of learning a subject. Others believe that students should first develop the basic skills without these tools.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    343 words

    An artificial intelligence tool can make a new subject easier to approach, while also making it easier to pass over something the learner has not understood. This is why there are reasonable arguments for both immediate access and an initial period of independent work. I favour early, guided access after learners have made a genuine attempt at the relevant task, with regular opportunities to work without the tool.

    Using AI from the beginning can help students who need an explanation at the moment a difficulty arises. A learner may ask for an unfamiliar term to be explained differently or compare two possible approaches to a problem. Such support can make a first attempt less discouraging and reveal questions the student had not known how to ask. Its value depends on the interaction: receiving a finished answer and examining an explanation are not the same learning activity.

    The argument for building basic skills first is therefore substantial. Students need enough understanding to recognise when assistance is irrelevant or mistaken. They also need experience of choosing a method, following it and finding where it fails. If a tool performs every uncertain step, the final page may look complete while the learner's understanding remains difficult to judge. An independent attempt gives both the student and the teacher something more informative to examine.

    A strict division between a tool-free beginning and later unrestricted use would still be too simple. Basic skills develop at different rates within the same subject, and suitable assistance varies by task. A teacher might ask students to draft an explanation unaided, use AI to identify possible weaknesses, and then revise it with reasons for their changes. A later unaided task can test whether the student has gained something transferable. This sequence keeps the learner responsible for the meaning of the answer.

    I would consequently allow AI early, but organise its use around active attempts, questioning and independent checks. The important foundation is not a prescribed number of weeks without technology. It is a growing ability to understand and evaluate the help being received.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0830

    Artificial Intelligence, Automation & Human Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some organisations produce large amounts of material using artificial intelligence but struggle to check it carefully before use.

    Why can checking this material become difficult? What can organisations do to improve the checking process?

    Answer

    334 words

    Producing a document and establishing that it is fit to use are different kinds of work. Artificial intelligence may increase the amount of material an organisation can prepare without increasing its capacity to check it. The resulting difficulty reflects volume, the nature of errors and the way responsibility is organised. Improvement therefore requires control over both production and review.

    Volume creates an obvious problem. If a team receives more reports than it can read carefully, a checking stage may remain on the timetable while becoming increasingly superficial. Fluent language can make this worse because a doubtful claim may not announce itself through awkward wording. Reviewing it can require subject knowledge, access to the original evidence and time to follow a chain of reasoning. A quick inspection of the finished paragraph may reveal none of these problems.

    Responsibility can also become unclear. One person may request the material, another edit its wording and a third approve its release, with each assuming that someone else has checked the substance. Repeated versions add further difficulty: a correction in one document does not ensure that related copies have changed. When performance is measured mainly by the quantity produced, careful checking can appear to be an obstacle rather than part of the task.

    Organisations should first limit production to material that serves a clear purpose and that they have the capacity to review. Each item needs an identifiable owner and checks suited to its consequences. A routine internal summary and instructions affecting public safety do not require identical procedures. Claims should be traceable to suitable sources, important calculations checked independently, and unresolved points kept visible until they are settled. Reviewers also need authority to delay or reject material, rather than merely improve its presentation.

    Finally, recurring errors should lead to changes in the production process. A checklist is useful only if the work it describes is actually performed. The objective should be a manageable flow of dependable material, with checking treated as part of making it ready for use.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0835

    Artificial Intelligence, Automation & Human Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    When an automated system makes a decision that seriously affects a person’s access to a public service, a named human official should remain responsible for that decision.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    334 words

    A person denied access to a public service needs to know who can explain the decision and put it right if it is wrong. An automated process should not remove that route. I strongly agree that a named human official should remain responsible for serious decisions of this kind, provided that responsibility comes with real authority, information and support.

    Automation can distribute a decision across several stages. Data may be collected in one place, rules chosen in another and an outcome issued elsewhere. Without a clear point of responsibility, an applicant may be passed between offices, each describing only its small part of the process. A named official gives the person somewhere to direct a question and makes it harder for the overall decision to disappear into the gaps between departments.

    This role must involve more than signing a letter. The official should be able to establish which information was used, consider relevant circumstances and arrange a meaningful review. Where an error is found, there must be a practical route to correction. It would be unreasonable to assign someone responsibility for a decision while denying them access to its basis or the power to change its consequences. A visible name without these abilities offers only the appearance of accountability.

    There are reasonable concerns about making one person answer for a complicated system. Technical staff, service managers and those who set eligibility rules have responsibilities of their own. Naming an official should not erase those duties or create a convenient individual to blame for institutional failures. The role should connect these responsibilities and ensure that the affected person receives a coherent response. Appropriate training, manageable workloads and records of decisions are therefore essential.

    I support named human responsibility as the public point of accountability within this wider structure. Serious decisions may use automated assistance, but the institution must still be able to hear a person's case. Responsibility is meaningful when somebody can act on the answer, rather than merely acknowledge that a question has arrived.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0838

    Artificial Intelligence, Automation & Human Skills

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people readily accept advice from an automated system, while others hesitate even when the same advice is also given by a person.

    Why might people differ in their trust? What information should users have before relying on automated advice?

    Answer

    331 words

    People can receive identical advice and judge it differently because trust concerns the route by which an answer was reached as well as the answer itself. Previous experience, expectations about machines and the possible cost of an error can all influence that judgement. Users therefore need information that helps them assess whether a particular automated recommendation fits their situation.

    Someone who has repeatedly received useful advice from a system may begin to accept its suggestions with little hesitation. Another person may remember a single serious error or worry that the system has overlooked something important. Some regard automation as consistent and free from personal prejudice; others are more comfortable questioning a person who can respond. Neither expectation is enough by itself to establish reliability. A human endorsement may reassure a doubtful user, but less so if that person appears merely to repeat the system's output. Two matching answers are more informative when they come from genuinely separate assessments.

    Before relying on advice, users should know what the system is intended to do, what information it has used and which relevant circumstances it cannot take into account. A recommendation about a training course, for example, may reflect a person's qualifications while overlooking their caring responsibilities or preferred kind of work. Users should also have understandable evidence of performance in comparable situations, including the kinds of mistakes that occur. A confident sentence on a screen is not a measure of accuracy, and a clear explanation of the reasoning is useful only if it represents the actual basis of the advice.

    Finally, the consequences of being wrong should determine how much checking is needed. Users need to know when independent advice is appropriate, how to correct inaccurate information and who can resolve a problem. They should also be free to reject a recommendation without being forced through unnecessary obstacles. These arrangements would support a more considered form of trust: one based on the system's purpose, demonstrated limits and relevance to the decision being made.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0842

    Scientific Research, Space & Public Investment

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that researchers should decide which scientific questions deserve investigation. Others believe that the public should have more influence over research priorities.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    343 words

    Choosing a research question involves judging both what can be investigated and what is worth knowing. Researchers bring essential knowledge to the first judgement, while the second can affect a much wider community. I believe researchers should retain substantial freedom to propose and assess questions, with meaningful public influence over broad priorities and the use of shared resources.

    The case for scientific independence begins with expertise. A question that appears simple may require methods that do not yet exist, while a seemingly remote problem may connect several important lines of inquiry. Researchers are well placed to assess these relationships and recognise when a field is ready to move forward. If every project had to promise an immediately visible benefit, difficult foundational work could struggle to begin. Its value cannot always be stated as a product that will arrive on a particular date.

    Public influence is equally important because specialists do not possess every kind of relevant knowledge. People living with a practical problem may notice needs that established research programmes overlook. Communities also have legitimate views about the burdens, risks and benefits associated with research. When public resources are involved, explaining how priorities are chosen can make those choices more accountable. Consultation can help researchers ask a better question, rather than simply obtain approval for one already fixed.

    The difficulty is designing participation that informs decisions without turning each technical judgement into a popularity contest. A small, vocal group should not automatically stand for the whole public. I would combine broad consultation with transparent expert assessment, and protect some funding for exploratory work. Researchers should explain uncertainty and feasibility in accessible language; public participants should have opportunities to discuss competing needs and revise their views. Neither side should be asked to perform the other's role without support.

    The best arrangement therefore shares influence while distinguishing responsibilities. Researchers should help establish what a proposed investigation could reveal, and the public should help shape which needs and questions receive attention. Clear reasons for the resulting balance matter more than assigning complete control to either group.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0850

    Scientific Research, Space & Public Investment

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Scientific discoveries can later be used for purposes that were not considered when the research began.

    Why might these unexpected uses emerge? Who should have the main responsibility for deciding how such discoveries are used?

    Answer

    334 words

    Research often begins with a particular question, while the knowledge it produces can later travel into circumstances its authors did not imagine. Unexpected uses emerge because needs, technologies and connections between fields change. Decisions about those uses should be led by accountable institutions and those responsible for implementation, informed by researchers and people who may be affected.

    One reason for unforeseen applications is that a discovery may describe a relationship more general than the original problem. A method developed to distinguish patterns in one kind of material might later prove useful with another. Its researchers cannot know every future setting in which the same relationship will matter. Further discoveries can also provide a missing component, turning an idea that was once impractical into an available technique. What becomes possible depends on more than the first discovery alone.

    Changing social needs create another route. People may return to existing knowledge when a new difficulty gives it a purpose. Contact between fields can reveal possibilities that remained invisible while each group worked separately. These developments do not necessarily show that the original researchers failed to think carefully. The relevant circumstances or combinations may not have existed when their work began.

    Responsibility for use should therefore follow the decisions that can actually be made. Researchers should explain the evidence, limitations and foreseeable risks of their findings. Those developing a particular application must assess its proposed setting and consequences. Where uses have serious public effects, accountable public bodies should set boundaries through informed, transparent decisions, with affected groups able to contribute. Leaving every decision to the original discoverer would demand knowledge and control that one person or team may not possess.

    I would give those public bodies the main responsibility for deciding which consequential uses are acceptable, while keeping developers responsible for their own choices. Scientific knowledge should inform that process without settling every ethical question. The discovery starts a chain of possibilities; each later decision still needs reasons suited to the people and circumstances it will affect.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0852

    Scientific Research, Space & Public Investment

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some universities are encouraging researchers from science, the arts and social subjects to work together on shared projects.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    319 words

    Some problems arrive without respecting the boundaries between university departments. Understanding them may require measurements, interpretation and attention to how people actually live. I regard encouraging collaboration between science, the arts and social subjects as a positive development, especially when it allows researchers to examine different aspects of one clearly defined question.

    The main benefit is that an apparently complete solution can be tested from another viewpoint. Consider a project to improve public warning messages. Scientific work might establish what information the warning needs to convey, while researchers concerned with language, design and social behaviour could investigate how different audiences understand it. An accurate statement that people cannot interpret is incomplete for that purpose. Collaboration can expose the missing connection before the work is treated as finished.

    Working across subjects can also make researchers more explicit about their assumptions. A term that seems ordinary within one discipline may carry a different meaning in another. Explaining it forces a team to distinguish what is established, what is inferred and what is simply conventional. This process may be slow at first, but it can produce a more carefully framed question and a clearer account of the evidence needed to answer it.

    There are costs, however. Different methods, timescales and expectations can make cooperation difficult. A shared project may also give one discipline the central decisions while asking the others only to improve its presentation. Universities should therefore provide time for genuine exchange, agree responsibilities and recognise contributions fairly. Collaboration should be encouraged where the question benefits from it, while allowing valuable work within a single field to continue.

    On balance, the development is beneficial. Its success should be judged by the quality of the inquiry and the understanding achieved, not by the number of departments listed on a proposal. The strongest projects allow another perspective to change the work itself, including what the researchers thought they were trying to find out.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0858

    Scientific Research, Space & Public Investment

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that researchers should be rewarded mainly for publishing new findings. Others believe that checking and repeating previous studies is equally valuable.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    332 words

    A new finding can open a field of inquiry, but its importance depends partly on whether others can rely on it. This gives checking and repeating research a value that novelty alone cannot supply. I believe researchers should be rewarded for both kinds of contribution, with the quality and significance of the work carrying more weight than whether its conclusion is new.

    There is a strong argument for rewarding discovery. New questions, methods and observations can make possible investigations that could not previously be attempted. Researchers may spend a long time developing an approach without knowing whether it will succeed. Recognition of such work helps preserve a willingness to explore uncertain ideas. A system that rewarded only confirmation would risk protecting established knowledge while giving too little support to its expansion.

    However, a published finding is also a starting point for further examination. Other researchers may need to determine whether the reported result can be obtained again, whether important conditions were omitted or how far the conclusion applies. A second study can repeat the question without merely repeating the work. Careful preparation, appropriate methods and an honest account of disagreement can all make a substantial contribution. An uncertain foundation affects what can safely be built upon it.

    Equal value does not require identical rewards for every new paper and every repetition. A weakly designed attempt to check a result is not valuable simply because it is labelled replication, just as novelty does not excuse poor evidence. Assessment should consider the importance of the question, the suitability of the methods and the clarity with which the work can be examined. Researchers should also receive credit for well-conducted checks that fail to confirm an expected result, rather than being pushed towards a pleasing conclusion.

    I would therefore give verification a recognised place alongside discovery in funding and career decisions. Research advances by extending what might be known and by improving confidence in what is claimed. A reward system should make room for both movements.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0859

    Scientific Research, Space & Public Investment

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people believe that research funding should mainly support projects likely to produce useful results soon. Others think that research with uncertain, long-term possibilities deserves equal support.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    349 words

    Research funding must answer needs that are already visible while allowing discoveries whose uses cannot yet be described. Projects promising useful results soon have a strong claim on limited resources. Uncertain, longer-term work also deserves substantial support, although I would not require the two categories to receive equal amounts regardless of the opportunities and needs involved.

    The argument for giving immediate usefulness priority is practical. Governments and other funders have problems to address now, and people may reasonably expect research spending to help. A project testing ways to make existing building materials withstand flooding, for example, offers a clear connection between investigation and a current need. Defined aims can also make progress easier to assess. When resources are scarce, funding a plausible improvement with a recognisable route into use may seem more responsible than supporting an interesting question with no foreseeable application.

    However, judging every project by its likely usefulness within a short period can narrow the questions researchers are able to ask. Investigating an unfamiliar property of a material may initially reveal only more questions. Those questions can still establish knowledge on which later work depends. Requiring a complete account of the future use at the beginning would favour projects whose destinations are already largely known. Supporters of equal funding therefore argue that uncertain work needs protection from a competition it is poorly placed to win: a promise of early benefit is easier to explain than a possibility whose shape remains unclear. This is a substantial argument for public support where commercial returns are especially uncertain.

    My preference is a balanced programme with a protected allocation for longer-term inquiry and enough flexibility to respond to urgent needs. Both kinds of research should face serious scrutiny, but the measures of progress should fit their aims. An exploratory project can be assessed through the quality of its methods and the knowledge produced without pretending that a marketable result is imminent. Equal respect does not require an unchanging division of money. Funding decisions should consider the strength of particular projects while preserving room for work that cannot promise a quick answer.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0875

    Inventions, Materials & Everyday Technology

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Before selling a product that depends on software, manufacturers should clearly state how long they intend to provide updates and support.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    323 words

    Manufacturers should clearly state their intended period of software updates and support before a customer buys a product that depends on them. I strongly agree with this requirement. The information affects the likely usefulness of the purchase, and customers should not have to discover an important limitation only after bringing the product home.

    For an ordinary physical object, a buyer can often inspect much of what they are paying for. Software-dependent products include a continuing relationship that is less visible. A device may be well made and carefully maintained, yet lose useful functions if associated software or services are no longer supported. Knowing the intended support period helps a customer judge whether the price is reasonable for the use they expect. Two apparently similar products may offer quite different prospects, and their purchase prices alone cannot reveal that difference.

    Advance disclosure would also make manufacturers explain what they mean by support. Customers need to know whether it includes fixing faults, addressing security problems, keeping essential services running or adding new features. These are different commitments. A clear statement should identify the planned end date and any important conditions, using language that a person can understand before buying. Placing an obscure qualification deep inside a long document would satisfy the appearance of disclosure while leaving the customer little better informed.

    Some manufacturers may argue that technology changes too quickly for a reliable prediction. That uncertainty is a reason to describe their plans carefully, rather than say nothing. An intended period is not a promise that every future problem can be solved, but it gives customers a basis for comparison and creates an expectation the company must take seriously. If plans change, customers should receive a clear explanation and timely notice. Overall, requiring this information would improve purchasing decisions without demanding endless support. It would make a continuing part of the product's usefulness visible at the point when the customer can still choose something else.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0894

    Sport, Fitness & Public Participation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some sports providers are replacing long membership commitments with activities that people can attend and pay for one session at a time.

    Is this a positive or a negative development?

    Answer

    337 words

    Replacing long sports memberships with sessions that people can book and pay for individually is generally a positive development. It lowers the commitment required to begin and makes organised activity easier to fit around a changing life. The arrangement needs careful management, however, if flexibility is to support continued participation rather than a succession of disconnected visits.

    The clearest benefit is that trying an activity becomes less costly and less daunting. Someone curious about badminton can attend a session, discover whether they enjoy the game and return with a better idea of what it involves. They do not have to predict several months of enthusiasm before picking up a racket. People with irregular work or caring responsibilities also gain a practical advantage. They can take part when time becomes available without paying throughout a period when attendance is impossible. This can make a provider welcoming to people who would hesitate over a long contract.

    There are disadvantages for both organisers and regular participants. A provider has to pay for space and staff even when fewer people turn up, so unpredictable attendance can make planning difficult. The price per visit may consequently be higher than the equivalent cost within a membership. Frequent users could end up paying more. Constantly changing groups may also make it harder to build friendships or provide instruction that progresses from one week to the next. In activities requiring practice, an isolated enjoyable session is only the beginning of learning.
