    These problems can be reduced without restoring lengthy commitments. Providers can use advance booking, offer transparent discounts for several sessions and publish a dependable timetable. They can also identify beginner and continuing groups so that people know where to return. Overall, the wider opportunity to participate outweighs the loss of some predictability, particularly for those previously excluded by cost or uncertain schedules. A successful service would combine the freedom to attend occasionally with a clear route towards regular involvement, allowing interest to develop through experience rather than requiring a long promise at the door.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0917

    Professional Sport, Competition & Sponsorship

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some sports allow officials to review video or other recorded information before confirming important decisions during a competition.

    What are the advantages and disadvantages of this approach?

    Answer

    335 words

    Recorded information can help sports officials make important decisions more accurately, particularly when an event happens too quickly to judge with confidence. Reviewing it can protect competitors from avoidable mistakes. The disadvantages are delays, disruption and the possibility of treating a recording as more conclusive than it really is.

    The strongest advantage is the opportunity to examine a decisive moment carefully. An official watching live must follow several moving players and may have a restricted view. A recording can allow another angle or a closer look at whether a ball crossed a boundary. When the evidence is clear, correcting the decision gives competitors a fairer result. It can also make the reasoning easier to explain: players and spectators can see the relevant event instead of being asked simply to accept an impression formed in a fraction of a second.

    However, the review itself changes the experience of the competition. Players wait while an energetic passage of play becomes a discussion around a screen. Spectators may celebrate, stop and then wonder whether to celebrate again. Repeated interruptions can weaken the rhythm of a match, even when each review concerns a potentially important decision. A more accurate decision about each moment does not automatically produce a better experience of the whole event.

    There are also limits to the evidence. A camera may miss the crucial view, and some decisions require an interpretation of conduct rather than a simple measurement. Slowing an action can reveal detail while altering the impression of its pace. Officials still need clear rules about what the recording establishes and what remains uncertain. Otherwise, the technology can give a disputed judgement an appearance of certainty without resolving the disagreement.

    Video review is therefore most useful for important, reviewable decisions under a clear procedure. Time limits, transparent explanations and a stated response to inconclusive evidence can preserve its benefits while reducing disruption. The aim should be fairer decisions within a playable and enjoyable competition, with recorded evidence used according to what it can actually show.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0926

    Leisure, Hobbies & Access to Recreation

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some towns close central streets to vehicles on selected weekends so that residents can use them for games, performances and other leisure activities.

    Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

    Answer

    336 words

    Closing central streets to vehicles on selected weekends can give a town a valuable shared space without building a new leisure facility. I believe the advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages, provided that access and displaced traffic are carefully managed. The temporary nature of the arrangement allows a town to gain something different from streets that already serve it throughout the week.

    The main benefit is the opportunity for ordinary public activity. Children can play a game, local musicians can perform and neighbours can stop for a conversation without competing with passing vehicles in the same space. People who would not join a club or travel to a distant venue may take part because the activity is nearby and easy to approach. A familiar street can also bring different groups together: someone who came to hear music may stay to watch a game or talk to a neighbour. Local businesses may benefit from visitors who spend longer in the centre, although increased trade is not guaranteed for every shop.

    The costs fall most heavily on people who still need to travel through or reach the area. Drivers may take longer routes, and nearby residential streets could receive extra traffic. A person with limited mobility may find a distant drop-off point a serious obstacle, even when the event is intended to be inclusive. Deliveries and residents' access also need practical arrangements. These difficulties deserve more than the assumption that everyone can walk a little further. A closure that creates a pleasant gathering place for one group can make ordinary tasks harder for another.

    Selected weekends give organisers time to plan around these needs. Clear advance information, accessible arrival points, suitable delivery times and monitored diversion routes can reduce the burden. Towns should consult affected residents and adjust the scheme if problems persist. With these measures, the recreational and social benefits justify the temporary inconvenience in many locations. The judgement should depend on the whole area's experience, including people attending the activities and those whose daily routes have changed.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0954

    Traditions, History & Social Change

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people keep objects from earlier stages of their lives even when the objects no longer have a practical use.

    Why do people attach value to these objects? What role can they play during periods of major change?

    Answer

    337 words

    Objects from the past can retain value long after they have finished the job for which they were made. A used ticket will no longer carry anyone on a journey, yet its owner may keep it carefully for years. Such objects can preserve connections with people, experiences and earlier versions of oneself. During major change, those connections can provide continuity and help a person understand what the change means.

    Their value often comes from a particular history. A ticket from a journey taken with a parent may recall the station, a conversation or the excitement of arriving somewhere unfamiliar. To another person it is a small piece of printed paper; to its owner it belongs to a larger event. An old school notebook can similarly preserve more than completed exercises. A teacher's comment in the margin, or an ambitious plan written on the last page, may bring an earlier concern or hope into view. The object supplies details that a general account of the past might leave out.

    These links can become especially important when familiar surroundings change. Someone moving to another country may unpack a few old belongings before the new room begins to feel their own. A person retiring from work might keep an object associated with colleagues as a reminder that those relationships formed part of their life, even when the daily routine has ended. The objects can also help people explain their history to others. A child asking about a worn badge may start a conversation that would otherwise never occur.

    This role is not always comforting. A possession can recall a painful period, and keeping everything may leave too little room for present needs. People may therefore choose a few meaningful objects or eventually decide to let them go. Their importance lies in the associations they carry, which can change as the owner changes. During an unsettled period, a carefully kept object can make the past easier to revisit and discuss, while leaving the person free to build a different daily life.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0962

    Time Management, Pace of Life & Priorities

    問題へ戻る ↗

    Some people think that reviewing how they spent the previous week is the best way to improve their use of time. Others believe that concentrating on plans for the coming week is more useful.

    Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

    Answer

    341 words

    A carefully written plan can become unrealistic before the first morning is over. Reviewing the previous week helps explain why, while planning the next week gives that knowledge a practical use. Both approaches are valuable, but I would give greater emphasis to forward planning, informed by a brief and purposeful review.

    Looking back can reveal patterns that are easy to miss while working. Someone may repeatedly allow an hour for a task that usually requires two, or discover that frequent interruptions consume the time reserved for concentrated work. A review can also challenge an unfair impression of failure. A week that produced few completed projects may nevertheless have involved important care responsibilities or unexpected problems. Understanding where time went makes it possible to distinguish poor organisation from demands that a person could not reasonably avoid. Without this evidence, the next plan may repeat the same mistaken assumptions.

    The case for concentrating on the coming week is that improvement requires decisions about what happens next. Planning allows people to identify priorities, reserve suitable periods for demanding work and arrange commitments before the available time fills up. It can also make trade-offs explicit. If two large tasks cannot both be completed, choosing which to postpone is more useful than carrying both forward as if determination would create another day. A plan gives people a basis for saying yes or no to new requests and for protecting time they need for rest.

    My preference is therefore to use review as preparation for a realistic set of choices. A few questions may be enough: what took longer than expected, what mattered, and what should change? The answers should lead to adjustments in the next plan, with some room for the unforeseen. Spending a long time recording every minute would offer little benefit if the same commitments were then accepted again. Conversely, detailed plans without any feedback can become repeated guesses. Forward planning deserves most attention because it directs action, but its quality depends on an honest, proportionate look at the week that has just ended.

    練習する · 語数・タイマー
    W2-0994

    Planning, Progress & Future Generations

    問題へ戻る ↗

    When choosing between policies with similar immediate benefits, governments should prefer options that leave future generations with more freedom to make their own choices.

    To what extent do you agree or disagree?

    Answer

    339 words

    When policies offer similar immediate benefits, governments should generally favour the option that leaves future generations more freedom to decide how they live. I strongly agree with this principle. People in the future will have needs and knowledge that present decision-makers cannot fully predict, and they should not inherit avoidable restrictions simply because one arrangement suited us.

    The value of flexibility is easy to see in public buildings. Two designs may provide equally good facilities now, but one may allow rooms to be altered or the building to serve a different purpose later. Future residents could then respond to changes in population or local needs without demolishing a useful structure. Similar reasoning applies to policies that create long commitments or make an existing arrangement expensive to change. When the present benefit is comparable, avoiding unnecessary dependence on a single future path is a sensible use of public resources.

    There is also a question of fairness. Future citizens cannot take part in today's decisions, although they will live with many of the consequences. Leaving them a reasonable range of choices acknowledges that their priorities may differ from ours. This does not require governments to predict what those priorities will be. It requires attention to decisions that close possibilities permanently and a good reason for doing so. A policy should not gain an advantage merely because its later restrictions fall on people who cannot yet object.

    However, freedom must be understood in practical terms. Future generations also need resources, dependable institutions and a usable environment if their choices are to mean much. A lasting commitment to protect an essential resource may limit one kind of activity while preserving many others. Governments should therefore assess the quality of the opportunities left behind, rather than count every possible action as equally valuable. Subject to that qualification, preserving future choice is a strong reason to prefer one policy over another when their immediate benefits are similar. It encourages decisions that serve present needs while remaining open to informed revision by those who come later.
